section: 15.1 3. Why raw data is never usable
text:
15.1 3. Why raw data is never usable
Preprocessing is turning raw data into a table an algorithm can read. It is most of the work in most projects.
Raw data is messy because it is produced by people and by imperfect machines:

somebody typed their age as 225
a sensor dropped offline and recorded nothing for four hours
one system writes dates as 10/05/2024, another as 2024-05-10
a customer pressed Submit twice
the “city” column contains Mumbai, mumbai, Bombay and MUM

An algorithm cannot see that these are problems. It will treat 225 as a real age and happily conclude that older customers spend more.

15.1.1 Demo 5 — watch one bad value ruin a summary

import pandas as pd

survey = pd.read_csv("datasets/survey_ages_typo.csv")
print(survey.to_string(index=False))

clean = survey["age_clean"]
typed = survey["age_as_typed"]        # respondent H's 27 was keyed as 225
print(f"\nAverage age, clean data     : {clean.mean():.1f} years")
print(f"Average age, one typo       : {typed.mean():.1f} years")
print(f"Median age, the same typo   : {typed.median():.1f} years  <- barely moved")

respondent  age_clean  age_as_typed
         A         25            25
         B         31            31
         C         28            28
         D         35            35
         E         22            22
         F         29            29
         G         33            33
         H         27           225

Average age, clean data     : 28.8 years
Average age, one typo       : 53.5 years
Median age, the same typo   : 30.0 years  <- barely moved


One wrong value out of eight moved the average by nearly 25 years. The median barely noticed. Session 7 explains why; Session 3 fixes the typo. For now, the point is only that raw data cannot be trusted.


15.1.2 Demo 6 — the same lesson, on a messier real file
Eight tidy rows made the point cleanly. datasets/messy_customers.csv — used again in Session 3 — has ten rows with a missing age, an impossible 225, and a negative -4, all at once. Does the same damage show up on a file nobody has cleaned yet?

messy = pd.read_csv("datasets/messy_customers.csv")
print(messy[["customer_id", "age"]])

all_ages = messy["age"]
plausible_ages = messy.loc[(messy["age"] >= 0) & (messy["age"] <= 120), "age"]

print(f"\nAverage age, all rows as typed      : {all_ages.mean():.1f} years")
print(f"Average age, only the plausible ones: {plausible_ages.mean():.1f} years")

   customer_id    age
0            1   25.0
1            2   31.0
2            3   28.0
3            4    NaN
4            5   22.0
5            6  225.0
6            7   29.0
7            8   33.0
8            3   28.0
9            9   -4.0

Average age, all rows as typed      : 46.3 years
Average age, only the plausible ones: 28.0 years


46.3 years against 28.0 years — an even bigger gap than the typed-survey example, because this file has two bad values pulling in different directions instead of one. Notice the file also has a missing age (NaN) sitting quietly in the middle of it; that one does not corrupt the average by itself, but it does mean .mean() is already silently dropping a row before you have decided whether that is the right thing to do.

title: 13  Session 2 — Data Collection and Pre-Processing Overview
text:
15.2 4. The order we clean in
The steps have to happen in a specific order. Running them in a different order produces numbers that look fine and are wrong.








#
Step
Chapter




1
Load the data
this chapter


2
Explore it — what is here?
this chapter, and Sessions 7–8


3
Duplicates — remove repeated rows
Session 3


4
Impossible values — an age of 225 is an error, not an extreme
Session 3


5
Missing values — decide what to do about blanks
Session 3


6
Outliers — decide about genuine extremes
Session 3


7
Combine other tables you need
Session 4


8
Encode and scale — turn text into numbers, put columns on one scale
Session 5


9
Reduce — drop or compress columns you do not need
Session 6









Important🔓 Two orderings that are not negotiable



Impossible values before missing values (step 4 before step 5). An age of 225 is a mistake. Turn it into “missing” first, then let step 5 deal with it. Do it the other way round and the mistake survives untouched into your model.
Scaling comes last, and only after the data is split for testing. Session 5 explains why, and shows the wrong answer you get otherwise.

title: 13  Session 2 — Data Collection and Pre-Processing Overview
text:
16.1 5. The Series and the DataFrame
pandas is the library that gives Python a table. A DataFrame is a whole table; a Series is a single column of one.
Plain Python can hold data in lists and dictionaries, but doing arithmetic across millions of rows that way is slow and awkward. Pandas does it in one expression.






Tip🧠 Analogy — a spreadsheet that takes orders



A DataFrame is a spreadsheet you talk to instead of click on. Instead of dragging to select rows 4–19, you say “give me the rows where city is Mumbai” — and it works the same whether there are 20 rows or 20 million.



16.1.1 Demo 7 — the smallest possible DataFrame
Before loading a file, it helps to see what a DataFrame actually is: a dictionary of columns, each one a Series, held together as a table.

import pandas as pd

tiny = pd.DataFrame({"fruit": ["apple", "banana"], "price": [40, 25]})
print(tiny)
print(f"\ntype: {type(tiny).__name__}")

print("\nOne column on its own is a Series:")
print(tiny["price"])

    fruit  price
0   apple     40
1  banana     25

type: DataFrame

One column on its own is a Series:
0    40
1    25
Name: price, dtype: int64


Two lists went in; one table came out, and pulling out "price" gave back a Series — the same shape pd.read_csv builds from a file. Every dataset in this book becomes exactly this: columns, held together, with a name for each one.


16.1.2 Demo 8 — building a table, and the column inside it

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.read_csv("datasets/shop_sales.csv")
sales["revenue"] = sales["units"] * sales["price"]   # a new column, computed for every row at once
print(sales)

print("\nOne column on its own is a Series:")
print(sales["revenue"])
print(f"\ntype of the table  : {type(sales).__name__}")
print(f"type of one column : {type(sales['revenue']).__name__}")

    product    city  units  price  revenue
0    Laptop  Mumbai      3  55000   165000
1     Mouse   Delhi     20    500    10000
2  Keyboard  Mumbai     12   1500    18000
3   Monitor    Pune      5  12000    60000
4     Mouse  Mumbai     15    500     7500
5    Laptop   Delhi      2  55000   110000

One column on its own is a Series:
0    165000
1     10000
2     18000
3     60000
4      7500
5    110000
Name: revenue, dtype: int64

type of the table  : DataFrame
type of one column : Series


The line sales["units"] * sales["price"] multiplied six pairs of numbers without a loop. That is the whole reason pandas exists.

text:
16.2 6. Looking at an unfamiliar dataset
Five commands tell you almost everything about a table you have never seen.







Command
Answers




.shape
how big is it?


.head()
what do the rows look like?


.info()
what type is each column, and how many values are missing?


.describe()
what are the numeric columns like?


.value_counts()
what values does this text column contain, and how often?




16.2.1 Demo 9 — the five-command first look
We load datasets/messy_customers.csv — ten rows of the kind of file a colleague actually sends you.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

messy = pd.read_csv("datasets/messy_customers.csv")

print(f"1. SHAPE — {messy.shape[0]} rows, {messy.shape[1]} columns\n")

print("2. HEAD — the first few rows")
print(messy.head(3))

print("\n3. INFO — types and how many values are actually present")
messy.info()

print("\n4. DESCRIBE — the numeric columns")
print(messy.describe().round(1))

print("\n5. VALUE_COUNTS — what is in the text columns")
print(messy["city"].value_counts())

2. HEAD — the first few rows

0            1  Asha   25.0  Mumbai  50000.0  2024-01-05        Yes
1            2   Brij  31.0  mumbai  62000.0  05/02/2024          Y

RangeIndex: 10 entries, 0 to 9
Data columns (total 7 columns):

---  ------       --------------  -----

 1   name         10 non-null     str    
 2   age          9 non-null      float64
 3   city         10 non-null     str    
 4   income       8 non-null      float64
 5   joined       10 non-null     str

dtypes: float64(2), int64(1), str(4)
memory usage: 903.0 bytes

4. DESCRIBE — the numeric columns
       customer_id    age    income
count         10.0    9.0       8.0
mean           4.8   46.3  162750.0
std            2.7   67.9  297998.0
min            1.0   -4.0   45000.0
25%            3.0   25.0   53750.0
50%            4.5   28.0   59500.0
75%            6.8   31.0   64250.0
max            9.0  225.0  900000.0

city
Delhi     3
Pune      2
Mumbai    1
mumbai    1
Bombay    1
MUM       1
delhi     1
Name: count, dtype: int64


Read the output and you have already found four problems, before writing a single line of cleaning code:

.info() shows age and income have fewer values than rows — some are missing.
.describe() shows max age is 225, and min age is −4 — both impossible.
.value_counts() shows Mumbai, mumbai, Bombay and MUM — one city, four spellings.
customer_id repeats 3 — a duplicate row.







Warning⚠️ .describe() only sees numbers



It silently ignores every text column. A dataset can look perfectly healthy in .describe() while its text columns are chaos. Always run .value_counts() on the text columns too.




16.2.2 Demo 10 — the same five commands, on a dataset with nothing wrong
It is worth seeing what a healthy file looks like through the same five commands, so you recognise “nothing to fix” as clearly as you recognise “something is wrong.”

inventory = pd.read_excel("datasets/inventory.xlsx")

print(f"1. SHAPE — {inventory.shape[0]} rows, {inventory.shape[1]} columns\n")
print("3. INFO — types and how many values are actually present")
inventory.info()
print("\n4. DESCRIBE — the numeric columns")
print(inventory.describe())

1. SHAPE — 5 rows, 3 columns

3. INFO — types and how many values are actually present
<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 5 entries, 0 to 4
Data columns (total 3 columns):
 #   Column   Non-Null Count  Dtype

dtypes: int64(2), str(1)
memory usage: 276.0 bytes

             price       stock
count     5.000000    5.000000

25%      60.000000   40.000000

Every column has 5 non-null values out of 5 rows — no gaps. price and stock have sensible minimums and maximums, nothing negative, nothing absurd. There is nothing here to call .value_counts() on either, since product is just five distinct names. A boring printout is itself an answer: this file needs no cleaning, and knowing that took the same five commands as finding four problems in messy_customers.csv.

text:
16.3 7. Selecting and filtering
Selecting is choosing which rows and columns you want. There are three tools, and they are easy to confuse.








Tool
Selects by
Example




df["col"]
column name
sales["price"]


df.loc[rows, cols]
label — the name of the row or column
sales.loc[2, "price"]


df.iloc[rows, cols]
position — the number, counting from 0
sales.iloc[2, 3]




16.3.1 Demo 11 — the three selectors, side by side

print("Whole column:")
print(sales["product"].tolist())

print("\n.loc — by label: row 2, column named 'price'")
print(sales.loc[2, "price"])

print("\n.iloc — by position: row 2, the 4th column (counting from 0)")
print(sales.iloc[2, 3])

print("\n.loc with a range — rows 1 to 3, two named columns:")
print(sales.loc[1:3, ["product", "revenue"]])

print("\n.iloc with a range — the first 2 rows, the first 2 columns:")
print(sales.iloc[0:2, 0:2])

Whole column:
['Laptop', 'Mouse', 'Keyboard', 'Monitor', 'Mouse', 'Laptop']

.loc — by label: row 2, column named 'price'
1500

.iloc — by position: row 2, the 4th column (counting from 0)
1500

.loc with a range — rows 1 to 3, two named columns:
    product  revenue
1     Mouse    10000
2  Keyboard    18000
3   Monitor    60000

.iloc with a range — the first 2 rows, the first 2 columns:
  product    city
0  Laptop  Mumbai
1   Mouse   Delhi








Warning⚠️ .loc includes the last item, .iloc does not



sales.loc[1:3] returns rows 1, 2 and 3 — three rows. sales.iloc[1:3] returns rows 1 and 2 — two rows. This catches everybody at least once. .loc follows label logic (“from this one to that one”); .iloc follows Python slicing (“stop before”).




16.3.2 Demo 12 — filtering with a condition
Filtering is the single most-used operation in pandas. You write a condition; pandas gives you back only the rows where it is true.

# The condition on its own produces True/False for every row:
print("Is revenue over 50,000?")
print((sales["revenue"] > 50_000).tolist())

# Put it in square brackets to keep only the True rows:
print("\nOnly the big-revenue rows:")
print(sales[sales["revenue"] > 50_000])

# Two conditions: & means "and", | means "or". Each condition needs its own brackets.
print("\nMumbai rows with more than 10 units:")
print(sales[(sales["city"] == "Mumbai") & (sales["units"] > 10)])

Is revenue over 50,000?
[True, False, False, True, False, True]

Only the big-revenue rows:
   product    city  units  price  revenue
0   Laptop  Mumbai      3  55000   165000
3  Monitor    Pune      5  12000    60000
5   Laptop   Delhi      2  55000   110000

Mumbai rows with more than 10 units:
    product    city  units  price  revenue
2  Keyboard  Mumbai     12   1500    18000
4     Mouse  Mumbai     15    500     7500








Warning⚠️ Use & and |, not and and or



sales[(a) and (b)] raises an error. Pandas compares whole columns at a time, so it needs & and |, and each condition must be in its own brackets — without them, Python’s order of operations gives you a confusing error.

16.4 8. Grouping: answering real questions
groupby splits the table into groups, applies a calculation to each, and puts the answers back together. It is how you turn a table of transactions into a summary somebody wants to read.

16.4.1 Demo 13 — from raw rows to an answer

print("Total revenue per city:")
print(sales.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False))

print("\nUnits sold per product, and the average price:")
print(sales.groupby("product").agg(
    total_units=("units", "sum"),
    avg_price=("price", "mean"),
    times_sold=("units", "count"),
))

print("\nRevenue by city and product together:")
print(sales.groupby(["city", "product"])["revenue"].sum())

product

city    product

summary = sales.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum().reset_index()

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
14.2 How this chapter is organised



Part
Question it answers




A — The order of operations
Which problem do I fix first, and why does it matter?


B — The six cleaning jobs
How do I actually fix each one?


C — The full pass
What does it look like done properly, end to end?



Part A is short and is the most important part of the chapter.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
15.1 1. Why order matters
Data cleaning is six jobs done in a fixed order.





flowchart LR
    A["1 Duplicates"] --> B["2 Impossible<br/>values"] --> C["3 Missing<br/>values"]
    C --> D["4 Noise"] --> E["5 Outliers"] --> F["6 Text and<br/>types"]






Here is why the order is not a matter of taste.
Suppose one customer’s age was typed as 225. That is impossible — nobody is 225.

Do it in the right order. Step 2 turns 225 into “missing”. Step 3 then replaces it with a sensible age, say 34. The mistake is gone.
Do steps 2 and 3 the other way round. Step 3 looks for blanks, finds none — 225 is a number, not a blank — and does nothing. 225 survives into your model and drags every average upward.







Important🔓 Impossible is not the same as extreme



Impossible = it cannot be true. An age of 225. A negative price. A blood pressure of 0. → It is an error. Turn it into missing, then impute it.
Extreme = unusual but real. A customer who spent ₹4,00,000. A 61-year-old marathon runner. → It is data. Think hard before touching it.
The dataset cannot tell you which is which. Only knowledge of the subject can.



15.1.1 Demo 1 — the same data, cleaned in two different orders

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

ages = pd.read_csv("datasets/messy_customers.csv")["age"].head(8)
print("Raw ages from the file:", ages.tolist())

# --- WRONG ORDER: fill the blanks first, then look for impossible values ---
wrong = ages.fillna(ages.mean())                 # the mean is already poisoned by 225
wrong = wrong.where(wrong <= 120, np.nan)        # now remove the impossible one
print(f"\nWrong order → mean used for filling was {ages.mean():.1f} (inflated by the 225)")
print("             result:", [round(v,1) if pd.notna(v) else None for v in wrong])

# --- RIGHT ORDER: remove impossible values first, then fill the blanks ---
right = ages.where(ages <= 120, np.nan)          # 225 becomes missing
right = right.fillna(right.mean())               # now the mean is honest
print(f"\nRight order → mean used for filling was {ages.where(ages<=120).mean():.1f}")
print("             result:", [round(v,1) for v in right])

Raw ages from the file: [25.0, 31.0, 28.0, nan, 22.0, 225.0, 29.0, 33.0]

Wrong order → mean used for filling was 56.1 (inflated by the 225)
             result: [25.0, 31.0, 28.0, 56.1, 22.0, None, 29.0, 33.0]

Right order → mean used for filling was 28.0
             result: [25.0, 31.0, 28.0, 28.0, 22.0, 28.0, 29.0, 33.0]


In the wrong order the blank was filled using a mean of 56.1, a value no customer is anywhere near, because the impossible 225 was still inside the average. In the right order the mean was 28.0. Same file, same functions, different order — and one answer is nonsense.


15.1.2 Demo 2 — the same file, but with a second impossible value too
The eight ages above only had one problem to catch. The full file has ten rows, and one more impossible age hiding in it: -4. A real rule has to catch both directions — too high and too low — not just the one you already know about.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

all_ages = pd.read_csv("datasets/messy_customers.csv")["age"]
print("All 10 recorded ages:", all_ages.tolist())

# WRONG ORDER: fill first, using a mean poisoned by 225 (and unaware -4 is a problem)
wrong_all = all_ages.fillna(all_ages.mean())
wrong_all = wrong_all.where((wrong_all >= 0) & (wrong_all <= 120), np.nan)
print(f"\nWrong order → mean used for filling was {all_ages.mean():.1f}")
print("             result:", [round(v, 1) if pd.notna(v) else None for v in wrong_all])

# RIGHT ORDER: a two-sided rule catches 225 AND -4 before anything is filled
right_all = all_ages.where((all_ages >= 0) & (all_ages <= 120), np.nan)
right_all = right_all.fillna(right_all.mean())
print(f"\nRight order → mean used for filling was {all_ages.where((all_ages>=0)&(all_ages<=120)).mean():.1f}")
print("             result:", [round(v, 1) for v in right_all])

All 10 recorded ages: [25.0, 31.0, 28.0, nan, 22.0, 225.0, 29.0, 33.0, 28.0, -4.0]

Wrong order → mean used for filling was 46.3
             result: [25.0, 31.0, 28.0, 46.3, 22.0, None, 29.0, 33.0, 28.0, None]

Right order → mean used for filling was 28.0
             result: [25.0, 31.0, 28.0, 28.0, 22.0, 28.0, 29.0, 33.0, 28.0, 28.0]


Doing it in the wrong order this time leaves two values permanently blank — 225 and -4 are caught too late to be filled at all, because the fill already happened. Doing it in the right order catches both, and every one of the ten customers ends up with a usable age.

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
16.1 2. Duplicates
A duplicate is the same real-world thing recorded twice. They arrive when somebody double-clicks Submit, when two systems are merged, or when an export is run twice.
They matter because every duplicate silently increases that row’s influence. One customer counted twice votes twice.

16.1.1 Demo 3 — finding and removing duplicates

print("Rows that are exact copies of an earlier row:")
print(raw[raw.duplicated()])

print(f"\nDuplicated customer_ids: {raw['customer_id'].duplicated().sum()}")

deduped = raw.drop_duplicates()
print(f"\nBefore: {len(raw)} rows   After: {len(deduped)} rows")

Rows that are exact copies of an earlier row:
   customer_id  name   age   city  income      joined subscribed
8            3  Chan  28.0  Delhi     NaN  2024-03-11         No

Duplicated customer_ids: 1

Before: 10 rows   After: 9 rows


drop_duplicates() keeps the first copy by default. When rows differ slightly — the same customer with an updated address — you usually want the latest instead:

# Keep the last recorded version of each customer, not the first:
latest = raw.drop_duplicates(subset="customer_id", keep="last")
print(f"One row per customer, keeping the most recent: {len(latest)} rows")

One row per customer, keeping the most recent: 9 rows




16.1.2 Demo 4 — seeing every copy, not just the extra one
Before deciding which copy to keep, it often helps to see all of them side by side. keep=False marks every row that belongs to a repeated key, not only the ones beyond the first.

print("Every row that belongs to a repeated customer_id:")
print(raw[raw.duplicated(subset="customer_id", keep=False)][["customer_id", "name", "age", "city"]])

Every row that belongs to a repeated customer_id:
   customer_id  name   age   city
2            3  Chan  28.0  Delhi
8            3  Chan  28.0  Delhi


Both copies of customer 3 are identical here, so keeping either one loses nothing. If they had differed — a changed city, say — this is the view that would show you what you are choosing between before you commit to keep="first" or keep="last".






Warning⚠️ duplicated() only catches exact copies



"Chan" and "chan " are different strings, so a row containing one is not a duplicate of a row containing the other. Clean your text first (job 6), then check duplicates again — the second pass usually finds more.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
16.2 3. Impossible values
An impossible value violates a rule you know about the world. Finding them needs no statistics — only a list of rules.



Column
The rule
Impossible




age
between 0 and 120
225, −4


price
at least 0
−50


percentage
0 to 100
130


date joined
not in the future
2031




16.2.1 Demo 5 — apply the rules, and convert violations to missing

df = deduped.copy()

impossible = (df["age"] < 0) | (df["age"] > 120)
print(f"Impossible ages found: {impossible.sum()}")
print(df.loc[impossible, ["customer_id", "name", "age"]])

df.loc[impossible, "age"] = np.nan     # not deleted — marked as unknown
print(f"\nAges now missing (was {deduped['age'].isna().sum()}, now {df['age'].isna().sum()})")

Impossible ages found: 2
   customer_id  name    age
5            6  Faiz  225.0
9            9  Isha   -4.0

Ages now missing (was 1, now 3)


Notice we did not delete the rows. The customer is real; only their age is unknown. Deleting the row would throw away their income and city too. Job 4 fills the gap.


16.2.2 Demo 6 — checking several columns at once
Real tables have more than one column with a rule. A dictionary of rules, one entry per column, checks all of them in a single pass instead of writing the same code out by hand for each.

rules = {
    "age": (deduped["age"] < 0) | (deduped["age"] > 120),
    "income": deduped["income"] < 0,
}
for column, violation in rules.items():
    print(f"{column:<8} impossible values found: {int(violation.sum())}")

age      impossible values found: 2
income   impossible values found: 0


Age has two — the same 225 and -4 as before. Income has none — nobody’s income is negative here, even though one income (₹9,00,000) looks unusually large. That is an extreme value, not an impossible one, and the outlier rules later in this chapter are where it belongs.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
16.3 4. Missing values
A missing value is a cell where nothing was recorded. Pandas shows it as NaN. Most algorithms refuse to run with any NaN present, so every one has to go — either by removing the row or by putting an estimate in.
Putting an estimate in is called imputation.






Tip🧠 Analogy — the missing jigsaw piece



A jigsaw with one piece missing. You can throw the puzzle away (drop the row), or you can look at the surrounding pieces and cut a replacement (impute).
Where it breaks down: a cut piece is visibly a substitute. An imputed number looks exactly like a measured one. Later readers cannot tell them apart — which is why we add a column recording that we guessed.



16.3.1 First, why is it missing?









Type
Means
Example
Safe to impute?




Missing at random
the gap has no pattern
a sensor glitched
usually yes


Missing for a reason
the gap depends on something else
older people skip the income question
be careful


Missing because of the value
the gap depends on the answer itself
the highest earners refuse to say
imputing hides the pattern





16.3.2 Demo 7 — four ways to fill a gap

income = df["income"]
print(f"Missing incomes: {income.isna().sum()} of {len(income)}\n")

print(f"1. Mean   → fill with {income.mean():>10,.0f}   (pulled up by the 900,000 earner)")
print(f"2. Median → fill with {income.median():>10,.0f}   (the middle value, ignores extremes)")
print(f"3. Mode   → fill with {income.mode()[0]:>10,.0f}   (the most common value)")
print( "4. Group  → fill with the median for that person's own city\n")

by_city = df.groupby("city")["income"].transform("median")
print("Filled by city median:")
print(pd.DataFrame({
    "city": df["city"],
    "income_raw": df["income"],
    "filled_by_city": df["income"].fillna(by_city),
}))

Missing incomes: 1 of 9

1. Mean   → fill with    162,750   (pulled up by the 900,000 earner)
2. Median → fill with     59,500   (the middle value, ignores extremes)
3. Mode   → fill with     45,000   (the most common value)
4. Group  → fill with the median for that person's own city

Filled by city median:
     city  income_raw  filled_by_city
0  Mumbai     50000.0         50000.0
1  mumbai     62000.0         62000.0
2   Delhi         NaN         45000.0
3  Bombay     58000.0         58000.0
4   Delhi     45000.0         45000.0
5     MUM     71000.0         71000.0
6   delhi    900000.0        900000.0
7    Pune     55000.0         55000.0
9    Pune     61000.0         61000.0


Which to choose:







Situation
Use




numbers, roughly symmetric
mean


numbers, skewed or with extremes — income, prices, house sizes
median


text or categories
mode (the most common value)


groups that genuinely differ — salary by city, weight by species
group median


more than about 40% of the column is missing
drop the column





16.3.3 Demo 8 — always record that you guessed

df["income_was_missing"] = df["income"].isna()          # remember, before filling
df["income"] = df["income"].fillna(df["income"].median())
df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(df["age"].median())

print(df[["customer_id", "age", "income", "income_was_missing"]])
print(f"\nBlank cells remaining: {df.isna().sum().sum()}")

   customer_id   age    income  income_was_missing
0            1  25.0   50000.0               False
1            2  31.0   62000.0               False
2            3  28.0   59500.0                True
3            4  28.5   58000.0               False
4            5  22.0   45000.0               False
5            6  28.5   71000.0               False
6            7  29.0  900000.0               False
7            8  33.0   55000.0               False
9            9  28.5   61000.0               False

Blank cells remaining: 0


That extra True/False column costs nothing and answers the question every later reader asks: “is this number measured or invented?”






Warning⚠️ Imputation always shrinks the spread



Filling twenty gaps with the same median puts twenty identical values into the column. The average barely moves, but the data now looks more consistent than it really is, and any measure of spread is understated. That is the price, and it is worth paying — as long as you know you paid it.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
16.4 5. Noisy data
Noise is small random error on top of a real pattern. A thermometer that reads 30.1°C, then 29.8°C, then 30.3°C, when the room is a steady 30°C.
Noise is not wrong data — nothing needs correcting. It is distraction: it hides the trend you are looking for. Smoothing averages nearby points to bring the trend back.








Method
How it works
Best for




Rolling mean
average each point with its neighbours
time series


Binning
group values into bins, replace each with its bin’s average
any ordered column


Regression
fit a line and read values off it
when you know the shape




16.4.1 Demo 9 — three windows on the same noisy signal

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sensor = pd.read_csv("datasets/sensor_readings.csv")
hours = sensor["hour"].values
reading = sensor["sensor_reading"].values
truth = sensor["true_temperature"].values   # we know this only because we simulated it

s = pd.Series(reading)
plt.plot(hours, reading, alpha=.35, label="raw sensor reading")
plt.plot(hours, truth, "k--", lw=1.5, label="the real temperature")
plt.plot(hours, s.rolling(5).mean(),  lw=2, label="rolling mean, window 5")
plt.plot(hours, s.rolling(25).mean(), lw=2, label="rolling mean, window 25")
plt.xlabel("Hour"); plt.ylabel("°C"); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

for w in (5, 25):
    err = (s.rolling(w).mean() - truth).abs().mean()
    print(f"window {w:>2}: average distance from the real temperature = {err:.2f} °C")
print(f"no smoothing: average distance from the real temperature = {np.abs(reading-truth).mean():.2f} °C")







Figure 16.1: The same sensor reading, smoothed three ways. More smoothing means less noise and more lag.





window  5: average distance from the real temperature = 0.77 °C
window 25: average distance from the real temperature = 2.29 °C
no smoothing: average distance from the real temperature = 1.36 °C








Warning⚠️ Over-smoothing erases the thing you were looking for



Look at the window-25 line: it is beautifully smooth and it arrives late at every peak, because it is averaging in temperatures from twelve hours ago. Smooth enough and a real spike — a fraud burst, a machine failure — vanishes entirely. The window is a choice between noise and lag, and there is no setting that avoids both.




16.4.2 Demo 10 — binning instead of a rolling mean
The mechanism table above named three methods; only the rolling mean has been shown so far. Binning groups the hours into blocks and replaces every reading in a block with that block’s own average.

# Split the 120 hours into 12 blocks of 10, and replace each reading with its block's mean.
bins = pd.cut(sensor["hour"], bins=range(0, 121, 10))
binned = sensor.groupby(bins, observed=True)["sensor_reading"].transform("mean")

err_binned = (binned - truth).abs().mean()
err_window5 = (s.rolling(5).mean() - truth).abs().mean()
print(f"Binning, blocks of 10 hours : average distance from the real temperature = {err_binned:.2f} °C")
print(f"Rolling mean, window 5      : average distance from the real temperature = {err_window5:.2f} °C")

Binning, blocks of 10 hours : average distance from the real temperature = 0.64 °C
Rolling mean, window 5      : average distance from the real temperature = 0.77 °C


Binning does even better here than the window-5 rolling mean — 0.64 °C against 0.77 °C — because it averages a fixed block instead of dragging in points from outside it. The trade-off moves rather than disappears: every reading in a block gets the same smoothed value, so binning is blind to anything that happens inside one block.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
16.5 6. Outliers
An outlier is a value far away from the rest. Unlike an impossible value it might be completely genuine.
You need two numbers from Session 7 to find them. Here they are in one paragraph.






Important🔓 Two ideas borrowed from Session 7



Quartiles. Sort the values. Q1 is the value a quarter of the way up, Q3 is three quarters of the way up. The gap between them, IQR = Q3 − Q1, is the range the middle half of your data occupies.
Standard deviation. Roughly, the average distance of a value from the mean. A z-score says how many standard deviations from the mean a particular value is.
Session 7 does both properly. Here we only need them to draw a boundary.










Rule
Flags a value if
Use when




IQR rule
below Q1 − 1.5×IQR, or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR
almost always — it ignores the extremes while measuring


Z-score rule
more than 3 standard deviations from the mean
the data is roughly bell-shaped




16.5.1 Demo 11 — the two rules, and why they disagree

income = df["income"]

# --- IQR rule ---
q1, q3 = income.quantile(0.25), income.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
low, high = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
print(f"IQR rule    → Q1={q1:,.0f}  Q3={q3:,.0f}  IQR={iqr:,.0f}")
print(f"              acceptable range: {low:,.0f} to {high:,.0f}")
print(f"              flagged: {income[(income < low) | (income > high)].tolist()}")

# --- Z-score rule ---
z = (income - income.mean()) / income.std()
print(f"\nZ-score rule → flagged: {income[z.abs() > 3].tolist()}")
print(f"              largest z-score present: {z.abs().max():.2f}")

IQR rule    → Q1=55,000  Q3=62,000  IQR=7,000
              acceptable range: 44,500 to 72,500
              flagged: [900000.0]

Z-score rule → flagged: []
              largest z-score present: 2.67


The two rules disagree, and the reason is important. The z-score rule uses the mean and the standard deviation — and the ₹9,00,000 earner has inflated both, so it makes itself look normal. The IQR rule uses quartiles, which the extreme value cannot shift. Prefer the IQR rule whenever you suspect outliers, which is exactly when you are looking for them.


16.5.2 Demo 12 — seeing them, and deciding what to do

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.4))
ax[0].boxplot(income, orientation="horizontal"); ax[0].set_title("With the high earner")
ax[1].boxplot(income[income < high], orientation="horizontal"); ax[1].set_title("With it removed")
for a in ax: a.set_xlabel("Income (₹)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"Mean income including it : ₹{income.mean():,.0f}")
print(f"Mean income excluding it : ₹{income[income < high].mean():,.0f}")
print(f"Median (either way)      : ₹{income.median():,.0f}")







Figure 16.2: A box plot draws the IQR rule. The dot beyond the whisker is the flagged value.





Mean income including it : ₹151,278
Mean income excluding it : ₹57,688
Median (either way)      : ₹59,500


You have four options, and deleting is the last of them:







Option
When




Keep it
it is genuine and it matters — fraud, a top customer, a failure


Cap it
it is genuine but distorting; replace with the boundary value


Transform
the whole column is skewed; a log transform tames it (Session 5)


Delete
you can show it is an error, and you say so in the report









Warning⚠️ In fraud data, the outliers are the answer



Every fraudulent transaction is an outlier. A pipeline that removes outliers by rule deletes every case you were hired to find — and reports excellent accuracy on what is left. Never remove outliers automatically. Look at them first.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
text:
16.6 7. Inconsistent text and wrong types
The same thing written four ways is four different things to a computer. Mumbai, mumbai, MUM and Bombay become four separate categories, splitting one city’s data into four thin slices.

16.6.1 Demo 13 — repairing a text column

print("Before:")
print(df["city"].value_counts())

city = df["city"].str.strip().str.lower()        # trim spaces, lower the case
city = city.replace({"mum": "mumbai", "bombay": "mumbai"})   # map known aliases
df["city"] = city.str.title()

print("\nAfter:")
print(df["city"].value_counts())

Before:
city
Delhi     2
Pune      2
Mumbai    1
mumbai    1
Bombay    1
MUM       1
delhi     1
Name: count, dtype: int64

After:
city
Mumbai    4
Delhi     3
Pune      2
Name: count, dtype: int64


Four spellings became two real cities. Note the order: strip and lower first, so that " MUM " and "mum" both reach the alias map.


16.6.2 Demo 14 — dates stored as text

print("The 'joined' column is stored as:", df["joined"].dtype, "— that is text, not a date")
print("Sorting text gives:", sorted(df['joined'].tolist())[:3])

df["joined"] = pd.to_datetime(df["joined"], format="mixed", dayfirst=False)
print("\nAfter conversion:", df["joined"].dtype)
print("Now we can do date arithmetic:")
print(f"  earliest join date : {df['joined'].min().date()}")
print(f"  latest join date   : {df['joined'].max().date()}")
df["join_month"] = df["joined"].dt.month_name()
print(f"  months present     : {df['join_month'].unique().tolist()}")

The 'joined' column is stored as: str — that is text, not a date
Sorting text gives: ['05/02/2024', '2024-01-05', '2024-03-11']

After conversion: datetime64[us]
Now we can do date arithmetic:
  earliest join date : 2024-01-05
  latest join date   : 2024-09-01
  months present     : ['January', 'May', 'March', 'April', 'June', 'July', 'August', 'September']


While joined was text, "05/02/2024" sorted between "2024-..." strings by character, not by date, and no arithmetic was possible at all. Converting types is part of cleaning, not a formality.






Warning⚠️ 05/02/2024 is ambiguous



Is that 5 February or 2 May? Pandas has to guess unless you tell it with dayfirst=. Getting this wrong shifts dates by months and produces no error at all. Always state the format when you know it.

title: 14  Session 3 — Data Cleaning
section: 17.1 8. Cleaning as one function, with a report
text:
17.1 8. Cleaning as one function, with a report
A cleaning pass should be repeatable and should report what it did. If it is a scattering of cells run in an order you no longer remember, nobody — including you next month — can reproduce the result.

17.1.1 Demo 15 — the whole sequence, with a report

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def clean(data):
    """Run the six cleaning jobs in order and return the result plus a report."""
    report = {}
    d = data.copy()
    report["rows_in"] = len(d)

    # 1 — duplicates
    d = d.drop_duplicates()
    report["duplicates_removed"] = report["rows_in"] - len(d)

    # 2 — impossible values
    bad_age = (d["age"] < 0) | (d["age"] > 120)
    report["impossible_ages"] = int(bad_age.sum())
    d.loc[bad_age, "age"] = np.nan

    # 3 — missing values (median, because income is skewed)
    report["blanks_filled"] = int(d[["age", "income"]].isna().sum().sum())
    d["income_was_missing"] = d["income"].isna()
    d["age"] = d["age"].fillna(d["age"].median())
    d["income"] = d["income"].fillna(d["income"].median())

    # 5 — outliers: flag, do not delete
    q1, q3 = d["income"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    hi = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
    d["income_is_outlier"] = d["income"] > hi
    report["outliers_flagged"] = int(d["income_is_outlier"].sum())

    # 6 — text and types
    city = d["city"].str.strip().str.lower()
    city = city.replace({"mum": "mumbai", "bombay": "mumbai"})
    d["city"] = city.str.title()
    d["joined"] = pd.to_datetime(d["joined"], format="mixed")
    report["cities_after_merge"] = d["city"].nunique()

    report["rows_out"] = len(d)
    return d, report


clean_df, report = clean(raw)

print("CLEANING REPORT")
print("-" * 34)
for k, v in report.items():
    print(f"{k.replace('_', ' '):<24} {v}")
print("-" * 34)
print(f"{'blank cells remaining':<24} {clean_df.isna().sum().sum()}")
print("\n", clean_df[["customer_id", "name", "age", "city", "income", "income_is_outlier"]])

CLEANING REPORT
----------------------------------
rows in                  10
duplicates removed       1
impossible ages          2
blanks filled            4
outliers flagged         1
cities after merge       3
rows out                 9
----------------------------------
blank cells remaining    0

    customer_id   name   age    city    income  income_is_outlier
0            1  Asha   25.0  Mumbai   50000.0              False
1            2   Brij  31.0  Mumbai   62000.0              False
2            3   Chan  28.0   Delhi   59500.0              False
3            4   Devi  28.5  Mumbai   58000.0              False
4            5   Esha  22.0   Delhi   45000.0              False
5            6   Faiz  28.5  Mumbai   71000.0              False
6            7   Gita  29.0   Delhi  900000.0               True
7            8   Hari  33.0    Pune   55000.0              False
9            9   Isha  28.5    Pune   61000.0              False


Notice what the report does not say. It does not say “the data is now clean”. It says exactly what was found and what was done, so a reader can disagree with a decision — which is the point.


17.1.2 Demo 16 — repeatable means the same answer every time
“Repeatable” is a specific claim, and it is checkable: run the same function on the same input twice and the report should not differ by a single number.

_, report_again = clean(raw)
print(f"Same report both times? {report == report_again}")
print(report_again)

Same report both times? True
{'rows_in': 10, 'duplicates_removed': 1, 'impossible_ages': 2, 'blanks_filled': 4, 'outliers_flagged': 1, 'cities_after_merge': 3, 'rows_out': 9}


It matches, cell for cell. A scattering of manually run cells cannot promise that — skip one cell, or run one twice, and the next person gets a different answer with no way to tell. A function is not just shorter to write; it is the only version you can trust to repeat.

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
section: 16.1 1. Why data is never in one place
text:
16.1 1. Why data is never in one place
Data integration is combining data from several sources into one view you can analyse.
It exists because organisations do not store data for the convenience of analysts. Sales sit in the sales system, support tickets in the helpdesk, web visits in the analytics tool. Each was built for its own job. The question “do customers who contact support buy less?” touches all three, and no single system can answer it.






Tip🧠 Analogy — the wedding guest list



One partner keeps family names in a notebook; the other keeps friends in a spreadsheet. Neither list is wrong. But you cannot count chairs, order food or print place cards until they are one list.
The painful part is not the copying — it is that “R. Sharma” and “Raj Sharma” might be the same person, or might be two people. That question is the whole of data integration.
crumbs: Part B — Making data fit to use

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
text:
16.2 2. The five approaches
There are five ways to combine sources. They differ in one thing: how much data you copy, and who does the translating.










Approach
What happens
Data is copied?
Good
Bad




Physical (data warehouse)
copy everything into one central database on a schedule
yes
fast queries; one place to look
data is as old as the last copy; expensive


Virtual (federation)
leave data where it is; a layer queries each source live when asked
no
always current; nothing to store
slow; breaks when any source is down


Application-based
each application translates and pushes its own data to the others
partly
no central system needed
every app must know about every other; n apps means many links


Middleware
one translation layer sits between sources and converts formats
partly
apps stay simple; one place to fix
the middleware becomes a single point of failure


Manual
a person exports CSVs and combines them by hand
yes
needs nothing; works today
slow, unrepeatable, and error-prone




16.2.1 How to choose





flowchart TD
    Q1{"Does the answer have to be<br/>up to the second?"}
    Q1 -- yes --> V["<b>Virtual</b><br/>query the sources live"]
    Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Will the same question<br/>be asked repeatedly?"}
    Q2 -- no --> M["<b>Manual</b><br/>a one-off export is fine"]
    Q2 -- yes --> Q3{"Many systems that must<br/>talk to each other?"}
    Q3 -- yes --> MW["<b>Middleware</b><br/>one translation layer"]
    Q3 -- no --> P["<b>Physical</b><br/>copy into a warehouse"]












Warning⚠️ Manual integration is where most reporting errors come from



Copying and pasting between spreadsheets leaves no record of what was done, cannot be repeated identically, and fails silently when a column shifts by one. If a manual integration is going to happen more than twice, write the code instead.

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
text:
17.1 3. Stacking versus linking
There are two different operations, and mixing them up is the most common beginner error.








Operation
Question it answers
Function




Stacking
“here are more rows of the same thing”
pd.concat


Linking
“here is extra information about the same things”
pd.merge



Two months of sales → stack. Customers and their orders → link.





flowchart LR
    subgraph S["concat — stacking"]
        A1["Jan sales<br/>100 rows"] --> C1["200 rows<br/>same columns"]
        A2["Feb sales<br/>100 rows"] --> C1
    end
    subgraph M["merge — linking"]
        B1["customers<br/>name, city"] --> C2["one row per match<br/>more columns"]
        B2["orders<br/>amount, date"] --> C2
    end







17.1.1 Demo 1 — stacking with concat

import pandas as pd

jan = pd.read_csv("datasets/sales_jan.csv")
feb = pd.read_csv("datasets/sales_feb.csv")
print("January:"); print(jan)
print("\nFebruary:"); print(feb)
print()

stacked = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True)
print(stacked)
print(f"\n{len(jan)} + {len(feb)} = {len(stacked)} rows. Columns unchanged: {list(stacked.columns)}")

January:
         date  amount
0  2024-01-05     250
1  2024-01-19      90

February:
         date  amount
0  2024-02-02     410
1  2024-02-27     130

         date  amount
0  2024-01-05     250
1  2024-01-19      90
2  2024-02-02     410
3  2024-02-27     130

2 + 2 = 4 rows. Columns unchanged: ['date', 'amount']


ignore_index=True renumbers the rows. Without it you get row labels 0, 1, 0, 1 — two rows labelled 0, which causes confusing errors later.






Warning⚠️ concat lines columns up by name



If one month’s file calls the column amount and the other calls it Amount, concat does not complain. It creates both columns and fills each with blanks where the other was used. Check .columns on both tables before stacking.



mismatched = pd.read_csv("datasets/sales_mar.csv")   # this file spells it "Amount"
print("March, as it arrived:"); print(mismatched)
oops = pd.concat([jan, mismatched], ignore_index=True)
print()
print(oops)
print("\nTwo amount columns, both half empty — and no error was raised.")

March, as it arrived:
         date  Amount
0  2024-03-01     500

         date  amount  Amount
0  2024-01-05   250.0     NaN
1  2024-01-19    90.0     NaN
2  2024-03-01     NaN   500.0

Two amount columns, both half empty — and no error was raised.




17.1.2 Demo 2 — the fix: rename first, then stack all three
Checking .columns found the problem. Fixing it is one line — rename the odd column out to match the others — and then all three months stack cleanly.

mar_fixed = mismatched.rename(columns={"Amount": "amount"})
all_three = pd.concat([jan, feb, mar_fixed], ignore_index=True)
print(all_three)
print(f"\n{len(jan)}+{len(feb)}+{len(mar_fixed)} = {len(all_three)} rows, "
      f"one column: {list(all_three.columns)}")

         date  amount
0  2024-01-05     250
1  2024-01-19      90
2  2024-02-02     410
3  2024-02-27     130
4  2024-03-01     500

2+2+1 = 5 rows, one column: ['date', 'amount']


One rename and the three-way stack behaves exactly like the two-way one did — a single amount column, no blanks, no silent duplication. The fix is always this cheap once you have actually looked at .columns.

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
text:
17.2 4. Linking tables with merge
merge joins two tables using a shared column called the key. The key is usually an ID.

17.2.1 Demo 2 — a first merge

import pandas as pd

customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/customers.csv")
purchases = pd.read_csv("datasets/purchases.csv")

print("customers:"); print(customers)
print("\npurchases:"); print(purchases)

joined = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="inner")
print("\nInner join:"); print(joined)
print(f"\ncustomers {len(customers)} rows + purchases {len(purchases)} rows → {len(joined)} rows")

customers:
   user_id   name    city
0        1  Alice  Mumbai
1        2    Bob   Delhi
2        3   Chan  Mumbai
3        4   Devi    Pune

purchases:
   purchase_id  user_id  amount
0          101        1   250.0
1          102        1   120.0
2          103        3    75.5
3          104        5   300.0

Inner join:
   user_id   name    city  purchase_id  amount
0        1  Alice  Mumbai          101   250.0
1        1  Alice  Mumbai          102   120.0
2        3   Chan  Mumbai          103    75.5

customers 4 rows + purchases 4 rows → 3 rows


Read that row count carefully. Four and four made three. Bob and Devi vanished (no purchases), user 5 vanished (not a known customer), and Alice appears twice (two purchases). This is normal, and it is why you check.


17.2.2 Demo 3 — seeing exactly which rows matched
Counting rows before and after tells you that something changed. indicator=True adds a column telling you which side every row came from, so you never have to guess.

tagged = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="outer", indicator=True)
print(tagged[["user_id", "name", "purchase_id", "_merge"]])
print("\nCount by origin:")
print(tagged["_merge"].value_counts())

   user_id   name  purchase_id      _merge
0        1  Alice        101.0        both
1        1  Alice        102.0        both
2        2    Bob          NaN   left_only
3        3   Chan        103.0        both
4        4   Devi          NaN   left_only
5        5    NaN        104.0  right_only

Count by origin:
_merge
both          3
left_only     2
right_only    1
Name: count, dtype: int64


both means the row matched on both sides. left_only is Bob and Devi — customers with no purchase. right_only is the purchase from user 5, who is not a known customer at all. This is the same information the row count gave you, broken down by exactly who is missing — and it scales to joins far too big to eyeball.

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
text:
17.3 5. The four join types
The join type answers one question: which rows do you keep when there is no match?








Type
Keeps
Use when




inner
only rows matching in both
you need complete records


left
all left rows; blanks where no match
the left table is your population


right
all right rows
rare — usually a left with the tables swapped


outer
everything from both
you are looking for what does not match




17.3.1 Demo 3 — all four, on the same two tables

for how in ["inner", "left", "right", "outer"]:
    result = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how=how)
    names = result["name"].fillna("(unknown)").tolist()
    print(f"{how:>6}: {len(result)} rows — {names}")

 inner: 3 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Chan']
  left: 5 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Bob', 'Chan', 'Devi']
 right: 4 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Chan', '(unknown)']
 outer: 6 rows — ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Bob', 'Chan', 'Devi', '(unknown)']


Now read what each one is for:

print("LEFT — every customer, whether or not they bought anything:")
left = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left")
print(left[["name", "city", "amount"]])

print("\nWho has never bought anything? The rows where amount is blank:")
print(left[left["amount"].isna()]["name"].tolist())

print("\nOUTER — everything, including the purchase by an unknown user 5:")
outer = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="outer")
print(outer[outer["name"].isna()][["user_id", "purchase_id", "amount"]])

LEFT — every customer, whether or not they bought anything:
    name    city  amount
0  Alice  Mumbai   250.0
1  Alice  Mumbai   120.0
2    Bob   Delhi     NaN
3   Chan  Mumbai    75.5
4   Devi    Pune     NaN

Who has never bought anything? The rows where amount is blank:
['Bob', 'Devi']

OUTER — everything, including the purchase by an unknown user 5:
   user_id  purchase_id  amount
5        5        104.0   300.0


The left join answered a business question the inner join could not: which customers have never purchased. An inner join deletes exactly those people.






Tip🧠 Analogy — the class register



inner — students who are on the register and sat the exam. left — the whole register; those who missed the exam show a blank mark. outer — the register plus any exam papers from people who are not on it.
The blanks are not a nuisance. They are usually the finding.




17.3.2 Demo 4 — what if both sides repeat the key?
Every example so far had a repeated key on one side only (Alice, twice, in purchases). What if customers also had a repeated key?

# Duplicate Alice's row once, on purpose, so user_id 1 now appears twice on the LEFT too.
customers_with_dup = pd.concat([customers, customers[customers["user_id"] == 1]],
                                ignore_index=True)
print(f"customers: {len(customers)} rows -> customers_with_dup: {len(customers_with_dup)} rows")

many_to_many = pd.merge(customers_with_dup, purchases, on="user_id", how="inner")
print(f"\n{len(customers_with_dup)} x {len(purchases)} -> {len(many_to_many)} rows")
print(many_to_many[["user_id", "name", "purchase_id", "amount"]])

customers: 4 rows -> customers_with_dup: 5 rows

5 x 4 -> 5 rows
   user_id   name  purchase_id  amount
0        1  Alice          101   250.0
1        1  Alice          102   120.0
2        1  Alice          101   250.0
3        3   Chan          103    75.5
4        1  Alice          102   120.0


Alice’s two customer rows each matched against her two purchase rows — 2 × 2 = 4 rows, where a clean key on both sides would have given 2. This is called a many-to-many join, and the row count is not additive, it is multiplicative: duplicate a key on both sides and the damage compounds instead of just adding up.

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
text:
17.4 6. Aggregate, then join
When one side has many rows per key, joining directly multiplies rows. Usually you want a summary instead.

17.4.1 Demo 4 — one row per customer

# Wrong for most purposes: Alice appears twice, so any count of customers is now wrong.
naive = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left")
print(f"Naive join: {len(naive)} rows for {len(customers)} customers")

# Right: summarise the many side first, then join one-to-one.
per_customer = purchases.groupby("user_id").agg(
    n_purchases=("purchase_id", "count"),
    total_spent=("amount", "sum"),
).reset_index()

summary = pd.merge(customers, per_customer, on="user_id", how="left")
summary["n_purchases"] = summary["n_purchases"].fillna(0).astype(int)
summary["total_spent"] = summary["total_spent"].fillna(0)

print(f"\nAggregate-then-join: {len(summary)} rows for {len(customers)} customers")
print(summary)

Naive join: 5 rows for 4 customers

Aggregate-then-join: 4 rows for 4 customers
   user_id   name    city  n_purchases  total_spent
0        1  Alice  Mumbai            2        370.0
1        2    Bob   Delhi            0          0.0
2        3   Chan  Mumbai            1         75.5
3        4   Devi    Pune            0          0.0


One row per customer, every customer present, spending totalled. This aggregate-then-join pattern is the one you will use most often in real work.


17.4.2 Demo 5 — what if you forget .reset_index()?
The aggregate above ended with .reset_index(). Skip it, and user_id stops being a column — it becomes the table’s index instead. Does the merge still work?

per_customer_noreset = purchases.groupby("user_id").agg(total_spent=("amount", "sum"))
print("Columns:", list(per_customer_noreset.columns))
print("Index name:", per_customer_noreset.index.name)

still_works = pd.merge(customers, per_customer_noreset, on="user_id", how="left")
print("\nMerged anyway:")
print(still_works)

Columns: ['total_spent']
Index name: user_id

Merged anyway:
   user_id   name    city  total_spent
0        1  Alice  Mumbai        370.0
1        2    Bob   Delhi          NaN
2        3   Chan  Mumbai         75.5
3        4   Devi    Pune          NaN


It works — pandas will match on="user_id" against an index name, not just a column name. But look at print("Columns:", ...) above: user_id is nowhere in it. Any other code that expects per_customer_noreset["user_id"] to exist — a filter, another merge, a plot — breaks, even though this particular merge did not. .reset_index() costs one line and removes the surprise.

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
text:
18.1 7. The three failures

18.1.1 Failure 1 — the key does not match
The most common cause of “the join returned nothing”. The keys look identical to a human and differ to a computer.

left_tbl  = pd.read_csv("datasets/subscribers_plan.csv")
right_tbl = pd.read_csv("datasets/subscribers_spend.csv")
print("The two files, side by side — the emails LOOK identical:")
print(left_tbl.to_dict("records"))
print(right_tbl.to_dict("records"))

print("\nJoining as-is:")
print(pd.merge(left_tbl, right_tbl, on="email", how="inner"))
print("→ 0 rows. One key has capitals, the other has a trailing space.\n")

for t in (left_tbl, right_tbl):
    t["email"] = t["email"].str.strip().str.lower()

print("After cleaning the key:")
print(pd.merge(left_tbl, right_tbl, on="email", how="inner"))

The two files, side by side — the emails LOOK identical:
[{'email': 'ASHA@mail.com', 'plan': 'gold'}, {'email': 'brij@mail.com ', 'plan': 'silver'}]
[{'email': 'asha@mail.com', 'spend': 900}, {'email': 'brij@mail.com', 'spend': 400}]

Joining as-is:
Empty DataFrame
Columns: [email, plan, spend]
Index: []
→ 0 rows. One key has capitals, the other has a trailing space.

After cleaning the key:
           email    plan  spend
0  asha@mail.com    gold    900
1  brij@mail.com  silver    400


Clean the key before you join. Trim spaces, fix the case, standardise the format. This is why Session 3 comes before this chapter.


18.1.2 Failure 2 — the same thing, different column names

orders = pd.read_csv("datasets/orders_by_ref.csv")   # this file calls the key cust_ref

merged = pd.merge(customers, orders, left_on="user_id", right_on="cust_ref", how="inner")
print(merged[["user_id", "name", "cust_ref", "total"]])
print("\n`left_on` and `right_on` join columns that mean the same thing but are named differently.")

   user_id   name  cust_ref  total
0        1  Alice         1    500
1        2    Bob         2    250

`left_on` and `right_on` join columns that mean the same thing but are named differently.




18.1.3 Failure 3 — duplicate keys multiply rows
This is the dangerous one, because nothing fails. The code runs, the model trains, the numbers look plausible, and they are wrong.

# A dirty reference table: 'Mumbai' is listed twice by mistake.
regions = pd.read_csv("datasets/regions_dirty.csv")
print(regions)
print()

blown_up = pd.merge(customers, regions, on="city", how="left")
print(f"customers: {len(customers)} rows  →  after joining regions: {len(blown_up)} rows")
print(blown_up[["user_id", "name", "city", "region"]])
print("\nAlice and Chan each appear twice. Every total computed from this table is now")
print("double-counted for Mumbai — and nothing raised an error.")

# The fix: make sure the lookup table has one row per key before joining.
regions_clean = regions.drop_duplicates(subset="city")
fixed = pd.merge(customers, regions_clean, on="city", how="left")
print(f"\nAfter de-duplicating the lookup table: {len(fixed)} rows")

     city region
0  Mumbai   West
1   Delhi  North
2    Pune   West
3  Mumbai   West

customers: 4 rows  →  after joining regions: 6 rows
   user_id   name    city region
0        1  Alice  Mumbai   West
1        1  Alice  Mumbai   West
2        2    Bob   Delhi  North
3        3   Chan  Mumbai   West
4        3   Chan  Mumbai   West
5        4   Devi    Pune   West

Alice and Chan each appear twice. Every total computed from this table is now
double-counted for Mumbai — and nothing raised an error.

After de-duplicating the lookup table: 4 rows

title: 15  Session 4 — Data Integration
section: 18.2 8. The check that catches all three
text:
18.2 8. The check that catches all three
One helper function, used after every join, catches every failure in this chapter.

def check_join(left, right, result, name="join"):
    """Report what a join did to the row count, and whether keys went unmatched."""
    print(f"{name}: left {len(left)} × right {len(right)} → result {len(result)}")
    if len(result) > len(left):
        print(f"  ⚠ GREW by {len(result)-len(left)} rows — the right table has duplicate keys")
    elif len(result) < len(left):
        print(f"  ⚠ SHRANK by {len(left)-len(result)} rows — some left keys had no match")
    else:
        print("  ✓ one row in, one row out")
    blanks = result.isna().sum()
    if blanks.any():
        print(f"  unmatched values appear as blanks in: {blanks[blanks>0].to_dict()}")

check_join(customers, regions, blown_up, "customers + dirty regions")
print()
check_join(customers, regions_clean, fixed, "customers + clean regions")
print()
check_join(customers, purchases, pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id"), "customers + purchases (inner)")

customers + dirty regions: left 4 × right 4 → result 6
  ⚠ GREW by 2 rows — the right table has duplicate keys

customers + clean regions: left 4 × right 3 → result 4
  ✓ one row in, one row out

customers + purchases (inner): left 4 × right 4 → result 3
  ⚠ SHRANK by 1 rows — some left keys had no match








Warning⚠️ A join that changes the row count is a claim, not an accident



A shrinking join says “these records had no match”. A growing join says “one of these keys is not unique”. Both may be fine — but you should be able to say which, and why, before you use the result.

title: 16  Session 5 — Data Transformation
text:
17.1 1. Why scale matters
Many algorithms measure distance between rows. A column with big numbers dominates that distance, whatever it actually means.
Consider two customers:




Age (years)
Income (₹)




Customer A
25
50,000


Customer B
55
51,000



To a human these people are very different — thirty years apart. To an algorithm measuring straight-line distance:

the age difference contributes 30
the income difference contributes 1,000

Income is 33 times more influential, purely because rupees are counted in thousands and years are not. The algorithm has not decided income matters more. It has been misled by a unit.






Tip🧠 Analogy — judging a competition in different units



Two judges score a contest. One scores out of 10. The other scores out of 1,000. Add the scores together and the second judge decides the winner every time — not because their opinion is better, but because their scale is bigger.
Scaling is making both judges score out of 10 before you add them up.



17.1.1 Demo 1 — watch a unit decide the answer

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

people = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_people.csv", index_col="person")
print(people)

def distance(p, q):
    return np.sqrt(((p - q) ** 2).sum())

print("\nRAW — who is A most similar to?")
print(f"  A to B: {distance(people.loc['A'], people.loc['B']):,.0f}")
print(f"  A to C: {distance(people.loc['A'], people.loc['C']):,.0f}")
print("  → B, because their incomes are close. Age was ignored.")

scaled = (people - people.min()) / (people.max() - people.min())   # squash both to 0–1
print("\nSCALED — the same question:")
print(f"  A to B: {distance(scaled.loc['A'], scaled.loc['B']):.2f}")
print(f"  A to C: {distance(scaled.loc['A'], scaled.loc['C']):.2f}")
print("  → C, a 26-year-old. Now age counts as much as income.")

        age  income
person             
A        25   50000
B        55   51000
C        26   90000

RAW — who is A most similar to?
  A to B: 1,000
  A to C: 40,000
  → B, because their incomes are close. Age was ignored.

SCALED — the same question:
  A to B: 1.00
  A to C: 1.00
  → C, a 26-year-old. Now age counts as much as income.


Same data, opposite answers. Nothing was corrected — a unit was simply stopped from voting twice.


17.1.2 Demo 2 — the same effect, across 600 customers
A three-person example could be a fluke. Here is the same question — “who is this customer’s closest match?” — asked for everybody in a bigger, more realistic file.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

cv = pd.read_csv("datasets/customer_value.csv")
X_raw = cv[["age", "income"]].values
X_scaled = MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(X_raw)

# For every customer, who is their single closest match — before and after scaling?
raw_match    = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=2).fit(X_raw).kneighbors(X_raw)[1][:, 1]
scaled_match = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=2).fit(X_scaled).kneighbors(X_scaled)[1][:, 1]

changed = (raw_match != scaled_match).mean()
print(f"{len(cv)} customers, matched by raw distance and by scaled distance")
print(f"Scaling changed the closest match for {changed:.0%} of them")

600 customers, matched by raw distance and by scaled distance
Scaling changed the closest match for 94% of them


This was never a three-person quirk. For almost everybody in this file, an unscaled distance calculation was quietly answering a different question than the one intended.

title: 16  Session 5 — Data Transformation
text:
17.2 2. Which algorithms care
Not every algorithm needs scaling. Knowing which is which saves work and prevents pointless transformations.








Algorithm
Needs scaling?
Why




k-Nearest Neighbours
yes
it is entirely built on distance


K-Means clustering
yes
distance again (Session 10)


Support Vector Machines
yes
distance to a boundary


Linear / logistic regression
usually
helps the fitting process, and makes coefficients comparable


Neural networks
yes
training is unstable otherwise


Decision trees
no
it asks “is age > 30?”, and that answer does not change with units


Random forests
no
many trees, same reasoning




17.2.1 Demo 3 — proving trees do not care

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

cv = pd.read_csv("datasets/customer_value.csv")
X = cv[["age", "income"]].values
y = cv["high_value"].values                          # the truth depends on income only

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
Xtr_s = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xtr)
Xte_s = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr).transform(Xte)

for name, model in [("Decision tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)),
                    ("k-Nearest Neighbours", KNeighborsClassifier())]:
    raw_score    = model.fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte)
    scaled_score = model.fit(Xtr_s, ytr).score(Xte_s, yte)
    print(f"{name:<22} unscaled {raw_score:.3f}   scaled {scaled_score:.3f}   "
          f"difference {scaled_score-raw_score:+.3f}")

Decision tree          unscaled 0.972   scaled 0.972   difference +0.000
k-Nearest Neighbours   unscaled 0.694   scaled 0.994   difference +0.300


The tree is unchanged. k-NN improves. That is the table above, measured rather than asserted.


17.2.2 Demo 4 — logistic regression, the “usually” case
The table calls linear and logistic regression a “usually”. Scaling rarely changes what they predict — but it changes what the numbers inside them mean.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

cv = pd.read_csv("datasets/customer_value.csv")
X = cv[["age", "income"]].values
y = cv["high_value"].values
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)
X_train_scaled = scaler.transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled  = scaler.transform(X_test)

raw_model    = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)
scaled_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print(f"Accuracy   unscaled {raw_model.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}   "
      f"scaled {scaled_model.score(X_test_scaled, y_test):.3f}")

age_coef_raw, income_coef_raw = raw_model.coef_[0]
age_coef_scaled, income_coef_scaled = scaled_model.coef_[0]
print(f"Unscaled coefficients — age: {age_coef_raw:.4f}   income: {income_coef_raw:.6f}")
print(f"Scaled coefficients   — age: {age_coef_scaled:.3f}   income: {income_coef_scaled:.3f}")

Accuracy   unscaled 0.989   scaled 0.983
Unscaled coefficients — age: 2.4866   income: 0.001245
Scaled coefficients   — age: 4.529   income: 4.394


Accuracy barely moves. But look at the unscaled coefficients: income’s is 0.001245 — not because income matters less than age, but because income is measured in tens of thousands and age is not. Scaled, both coefficients sit on the same footing (4.529 and 4.394) and can be compared directly. That is what “usually helps” means here: much the same predictions, far more readable coefficients.

title: 16  Session 5 — Data Transformation
text:
18.1 3. The five tools
Scikit-learn provides five transformers. Four work down columns; one works across rows. That distinction confuses everybody once.









Tool
What it produces
Works on
Use when




MinMaxScaler
every value between 0 and 1
columns
you want a fixed, bounded range


StandardScaler
mean 0, standard deviation 1
columns
the default choice


RobustScaler
centred on the median, scaled by the IQR
columns
outliers are present and you kept them


Normalizer
each row rescaled to length 1
rows
the proportions in a row matter, not the totals


Binarizer
0 or 1, split at a threshold
columns
you only care whether a value is above a line









Important🔓 ‘Normalizing’ means two different things



In everyday speech, “normalising” often means “putting on a 0–1 scale” — which is what MinMaxScaler does.
In scikit-learn, Normalizer does something else entirely: it rescales each row so the row’s values sum to a fixed length. It is used for things like word counts, where a long document and a short document should be comparable by proportion.
They are different operations in different directions. When someone says “normalise the data”, ask which they mean.



18.1.1 Demo 5 — all five, on the same small table

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import (MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler, RobustScaler,
                                   Normalizer, Binarizer)

data = pd.read_csv("datasets/six_earners.csv")     # six people, one of them a high earner
print("ORIGINAL"); print(data)

for name, tool in [("MinMaxScaler  (0 to 1)", MinMaxScaler()),
                   ("StandardScaler (mean 0)", StandardScaler()),
                   ("RobustScaler  (median 0)", RobustScaler())]:
    out = pd.DataFrame(tool.fit_transform(data), columns=data.columns)
    print(f"\n{name}"); print(out.round(2))

ORIGINAL
   age  income
0   25   30000
1   32   42000
2   47   61000
3   51   58000
4   62  250000
5   29   35000

MinMaxScaler  (0 to 1)
    age  income
0  0.00    0.00
1  0.19    0.05
2  0.59    0.14
3  0.70    0.13
4  1.00    1.00
5  0.11    0.02

StandardScaler (mean 0)
    age  income
0 -1.20   -0.64
1 -0.68   -0.48
2  0.45   -0.24
3  0.75   -0.28
4  1.58    2.21
5 -0.90   -0.57

RobustScaler  (median 0)
    age  income
0 -0.72   -0.85
1 -0.37   -0.34
2  0.37    0.47
3  0.57    0.34
4  1.11    8.51
5 -0.52   -0.64


Look at what the outlier does to each one:

for name, tool in [("MinMax", MinMaxScaler()), ("Standard", StandardScaler()),
                   ("Robust", RobustScaler())]:
    income_scaled = tool.fit_transform(data)[:, 1]     # the income column only
    ordinary = np.sort(income_scaled)[:-1]             # everyone except the highest earner
    print(f"{name:<9} income → range {income_scaled.min():6.2f} to {income_scaled.max():6.2f} ; "
          f"the five ordinary earners now sit between {ordinary.min():.2f} and {ordinary.max():.2f}")

MinMax    income → range   0.00 to   1.00 ; the five ordinary earners now sit between 0.00 and 0.14
Standard  income → range  -0.64 to   2.21 ; the five ordinary earners now sit between -0.64 and -0.24
Robust    income → range  -0.85 to   8.51 ; the five ordinary earners now sit between -0.85 and 0.47


MinMaxScaler is the one the outlier hurts most: the ₹2,50,000 earner takes the value 1.0 and squashes everybody else into the bottom seventh of the range. RobustScaler uses the median and the IQR, which the outlier cannot move, so ordinary earners keep their spread.


18.1.2 Demo 6 — Normalizer and Binarizer, which do something different

import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import Normalizer, Binarizer

# Normalizer works ACROSS a row. Here: word counts in two documents.
wc = pd.read_csv("datasets/word_counts.csv", index_col="document")
docs = wc.values
print("Raw word counts (datasets/word_counts.csv):"); print(wc)
print("\nAfter Normalizer — the two documents are now identical, as they should be:")
print(Normalizer().fit_transform(docs).round(3))

# Binarizer: above the line or below it.
scores = pd.read_csv("datasets/exam_marks.csv")[["mark"]].values
print("\nExam marks:", scores.ravel().tolist())
print("Pass (1) or fail (0) at 50:", Binarizer(threshold=50).fit_transform(scores).ravel().tolist())

Raw word counts (datasets/word_counts.csv):
          data  model  python
document                     
short        3      1       0
long        30     10       0

After Normalizer — the two documents are now identical, as they should be:
[[0.949 0.316 0.   ]
 [0.949 0.316 0.   ]]

Exam marks: [35, 52, 67, 40, 88]
Pass (1) or fail (0) at 50: [0, 1, 1, 0, 1]




18.1.3 Demo 7 — scaling changes the axis, not the shape

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

income = pd.read_csv("datasets/skewed_incomes.csv")[["income"]].values
scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(income)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax[0].hist(income, bins=40); ax[0].set_title("Before"); ax[0].set_xlabel("Income (₹)")
ax[1].hist(scaled, bins=40); ax[1].set_title("After StandardScaler"); ax[1].set_xlabel("Standard deviations")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"Before: mean {income.mean():>10,.0f}   std {income.std():>10,.0f}   skew stays the same")
print(f"After : mean {scaled.mean():>10.2f}   std {scaled.std():>10.2f}")







Figure 18.1: Before and after standardizing. The distribution’s shape is identical; only the numbers on the x-axis changed.





Before: mean     39,469   std     27,531   skew stays the same
After : mean       0.00   std       1.00








Warning⚠️ Scaling does not make data normal



Both histograms lean the same way. Scaling shifts and stretches; it does not reshape. If a column is heavily skewed and you need it symmetric, you need a different tool — a log transform:

print("Skewness before log transform:", float(pd.Series(income.ravel()).skew().round(2)))
print("Skewness after  log transform:", float(pd.Series(np.log1p(income.ravel())).skew().round(2)))

Skewness before log transform: 1.36
Skewness after  log transform: -1.01

title: 16  Session 5 — Data Transformation
text:
19.1 4. Encoding categories
Algorithms do arithmetic. They cannot do arithmetic on the word “Mumbai”. Encoding turns categories into numbers — and the method has to match the kind of category.









Kind
Meaning
Example
Encode with




Nominal
no order
city, colour, brand
one-hot


Ordinal
a real order
small < medium < large
ordinal


The target
what you are predicting
approved / rejected
label




19.1.1 Demo 8 — the three encodings, and the trap in the middle

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder, OrdinalEncoder

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/encoding_example.csv")
print(df)

# 1. LABEL ENCODING — one number per category. Correct for the TARGET only.
le = LabelEncoder()
df["approved_num"] = le.fit_transform(df["approved"])
print(f"\nLabel encoding the target: {dict(zip(le.classes_, range(len(le.classes_))))}")

# 2. ORDINAL ENCODING — for categories with a genuine order. You supply the order.
oe = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["small", "medium", "large"]])
df["size_num"] = oe.fit_transform(df[["size"]]).astype(int)
print("\nOrdinal encoding 'size' (small=0 < medium=1 < large=2):")
print(df[["size", "size_num"]])

# 3. ONE-HOT ENCODING — for categories with no order. One column per value.
print("\nOne-hot encoding 'city':")
print(pd.get_dummies(df["city"], prefix="city").astype(int))

     city    size approved
0  Mumbai   small      yes
1   Delhi   large       no
2    Pune  medium      yes
3  Mumbai  medium      yes
4   Delhi   small       no

Label encoding the target: {'no': 0, 'yes': 1}

Ordinal encoding 'size' (small=0 < medium=1 < large=2):
     size  size_num
0   small         0
1   large         2
2  medium         1
3  medium         1
4   small         0

One-hot encoding 'city':
   city_Delhi  city_Mumbai  city_Pune
0           0            1          0
1           1            0          0
2           0            0          1
3           0            1          0
4           1            0          0








Warning⚠️ Never label-encode a nominal feature



Label-encode city and you get Delhi = 0, Mumbai = 1, Pune = 2. The algorithm then believes Pune is twice Mumbai, and that Mumbai sits between Delhi and Pune. None of that is true, and the model will act on it.
Nominal features get one-hot encoding. The cost is one column per category, which is why a column with 5,000 distinct values needs a different approach entirely.




19.1.2 Demo 9 — the invented ordering, measured

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# The truth in this file: Mumbai is expensive, the other two are similar.
# There is no ordering among the three cities.
cr = pd.read_csv("datasets/city_rent.csv")
city, rent = cr["city"].values, cr["rent"].values

label = pd.Series(city).map({"Delhi": 0, "Mumbai": 1, "Pune": 2}).values.reshape(-1, 1)
onehot = pd.get_dummies(city).astype(int).values

for name, X in [("label encoded (wrong)", label), ("one-hot encoded (right)", onehot)]:
    r2 = LinearRegression().fit(X, rent).score(X, rent)
    print(f"{name:<26} explains {r2:6.1%} of the variation in rent")

label encoded (wrong)      explains   0.0% of the variation in rent
one-hot encoded (right)    explains  96.5% of the variation in rent


The label-encoded version does badly because it has been forced to fit a straight line through an ordering that does not exist. One-hot encoding lets each city have its own value, which is the truth.
