text:
20.1 🎯 Learning outcomes
By the end of this chapter you can:

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
Explain supervised learning and why it needs labelled data.
Tell a regression problem from a classification problem.
Fit a simple linear regression and read its slope and intercept as a sentence.
Fit a multiple regression and interpret a coefficient correctly.
Report MAE, RMSE and R², and say which to quote to whom.
Compare a model against a baseline and say whether it earned its place.
Name three assumptions linear regression makes and check one.

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
20.2 How this chapter is organised



Part
Question it answers




A — What supervised learning is
How does a machine learn from examples?


B — Simple regression
How do I predict a number from one input?


C — Multiple regression
And from several inputs?


D — Measuring it
Is the prediction any good?

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
21.1 1. Learning from labelled examples
Supervised learning trains an algorithm on historical data where the answer is already known. The known answer is called the label or the target.
You do not tell the algorithm the rule. You show it thousands of examples with their answers, and it works the rule out.






Tip🧠 Analogy — flashcards



A student revising with flashcards:

the front of the card is the input — the features
the back is the answer — the label
learning is guessing, flipping the card, and adjusting

Where it breaks down: a student understands why the answer is what it is. A model only finds a pattern that fits. Show it enough cards where the answer happens to correlate with the card’s colour, and it will learn colour.


The two vocabulary words used everywhere from here on:



Word
Means
Written as




Features
the inputs you know
X — a table, capital X


Target
the answer you want
y — one column, lowercase y

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
21.2 2. Regression or classification?
Every supervised problem is one of two kinds, decided entirely by what the target looks like.










Target is
Question
Examples




Regression
a number
how much? how many?
house price, tomorrow’s temperature, delivery time


Classification
a category
which one? yes or no?
spam or not, will they default, which disease



This chapter is regression. Session 10’s clustering and later work covers the rest.

21.2.1 Demo 1 — telling them apart

problems = [
    ("Predict a flat's monthly rent",                 "₹28,400",        "number"),
    ("Will this customer cancel their subscription?", "yes / no",       "category"),
    ("How many units will we sell next month?",       "1,840",          "number"),
    ("Which of 5 categories is this news article?",   "sport",          "category"),
    ("What score out of 10 will this film get?",      "7.3",            "number"),
]
print(f"{'problem':<48} {'answer looks like':<18} {'task'}")
print("-" * 84)
for q, example, kind in problems:
    label = "REGRESSION" if kind == "number" else "CLASSIFICATION"
    print(f"{q:<48} {example:<18} {label}")

problem                                          answer looks like  task
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Predict a flat's monthly rent                    ₹28,400            REGRESSION
Will this customer cancel their subscription?    yes / no           CLASSIFICATION
How many units will we sell next month?          1,840              REGRESSION
Which of 5 categories is this news article?      sport              CLASSIFICATION
What score out of 10 will this film get?         7.3                REGRESSION


That table was hand-built to make the point. Real columns need a real check.


21.2.2 Demo 2 — the same test on real columns

import pandas as pd

homes = pd.read_csv("datasets/house_prices.csv")   # used properly from Part C onward
churn = pd.read_csv("datasets/telecom_churn.csv")  # a fresh dataset, just for this contrast

print(f"price   : {homes['price'].nunique()} distinct values  → looks like REGRESSION")
print(f"churned : {churn['churned'].nunique()} distinct values → looks like CLASSIFICATION")

price   : 385 distinct values  → looks like REGRESSION
churned : 2 distinct values → looks like CLASSIFICATION


Counting distinct values is a quick, useful first check — a column with hundreds of different numbers is very unlikely to be a category, and a column with two values is very unlikely to be a continuous measurement.


21.2.3 Demo 3 — why counting distinct values is not enough

distinct_bedrooms = sorted(int(b) for b in homes["bedrooms"].unique())
print(f"bedrooms: {homes['bedrooms'].nunique()} distinct values → {distinct_bedrooms}")

bedrooms: 5 distinct values → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]


bedrooms has only 5 distinct values — as few as a 5-category classification target would have. Counting alone cannot settle this one. bedrooms is still a genuine count (five bedrooms really is two more than three), so treating it as a number is a safe call — Part C fits a regression on it. A satisfaction rating from 1 to 5 has exactly the same shape of data and a much shakier claim behind it. The check that actually matters is the one below.






Warning⚠️ A number is not always a regression target



A rating of 1 to 5 looks numeric. But if the gap between 1 and 2 does not mean the same as the gap between 4 and 5, treating it as a number is a claim about the world you may not want to make. Ask what the number measures, not what type it is stored as.

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
22.1 3. One input, one line
Simple linear regression draws the single straight line that comes closest to all your data points, and uses it to predict.
The line is described by two numbers:
\[\text{prediction} = \text{intercept} + \text{slope} \times \text{input}\]







Number
Means




slope
how much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in the input


intercept
the prediction when the input is zero



“Closest” has a precise meaning: the line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances to the points as small as possible. Squared, for the same reason as in Session 7 — so that errors above and below the line cannot cancel out.

22.1.1 Demo 4 — fitting one line, and reading it out loud

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

import pandas as pd

emp = pd.read_csv("datasets/experience_salary.csv")
experience, salary = emp["experience_years"].values, emp["salary"].values
print(emp.head(3), f"\n\n{len(emp)} employees on file\n")

X = experience.reshape(-1, 1)          # scikit-learn wants a 2-D table, even for one column
y = salary

model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
line = model.predict(X)

plt.scatter(experience, salary, s=25, label="actual people")
order = np.argsort(experience)
plt.plot(experience[order], line[order], "r-", lw=2, label="the fitted line")
for xi, yi, pi in zip(experience, salary, line):
    plt.plot([xi, xi], [yi, pi], color="grey", lw=.6, alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("Years of experience"); plt.ylabel("Salary (₹)"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"intercept = ₹{model.intercept_:,.0f}")
print(f"slope     = ₹{model.coef_[0]:,.0f} per year of experience")
print(f"\nRead as a sentence:")
print(f'  "Someone with no experience earns about ₹{model.intercept_:,.0f}.')
print(f'   Each additional year is worth about ₹{model.coef_[0]:,.0f}."')

   experience_years    salary
0             13.55  121356.0
1              1.02   31755.0
2             10.09  123457.0 

40 employees on file









Figure 22.1: The line of best fit. Grey lines are the residuals — the errors the fit is minimising.





intercept = ₹18,241
slope     = ₹9,725 per year of experience

Read as a sentence:
  "Someone with no experience earns about ₹18,241.
   Each additional year is worth about ₹9,725."




22.1.2 Demo 5 — using it to predict

import pandas as pd

for years in [0, 3, 7, 12]:
    pred = model.predict([[years]])[0]
    print(f"{years:>2} years of experience → predicted salary ₹{pred:>9,.0f}")

print(f"\n40 years of experience → ₹{model.predict([[40]])[0]:,.0f}")
print("  ⚠ nobody in the training data had more than 15 years. This number is a")
print("    guess about territory the model has never seen — it is extrapolation.")

 0 years of experience → predicted salary ₹   18,241
 3 years of experience → predicted salary ₹   47,417
 7 years of experience → predicted salary ₹   86,318
12 years of experience → predicted salary ₹  134,944

40 years of experience → ₹407,253
  ⚠ nobody in the training data had more than 15 years. This number is a
    guess about territory the model has never seen — it is extrapolation.








Warning⚠️ The intercept is often meaningless



Here “zero years of experience” is a real situation, so the intercept means something. But in a model predicting house price from area, the intercept is the price of a house with zero square feet — a number the maths needs and the world does not have.
Do not report an intercept as a finding unless zero is a real value for that input.

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
23.1 4. Several inputs at once
Multiple regression uses two or more features. Instead of a line through a scatter plot, it fits a flat surface through a cloud — but the code is identical, and so is the interpretation, with one crucial addition.
\[\text{price} = \text{intercept} + b_1 \times \text{area} + b_2 \times \text{bedrooms} + b_3 \times \text{age}\]






Important🔓 What a coefficient means, exactly



A coefficient is the effect of that feature while every other feature is held constant.
That phrase is the whole thing. “Each extra bedroom adds ₹4 lakh” is wrong. “Each extra bedroom adds ₹4 lakh, comparing houses of the same area and age” is right — and it is a completely different claim, because bigger houses usually have more bedrooms anyway.



23.1.1 Demo 6 — a real multiple regression, done properly

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

homes = pd.read_csv("datasets/house_prices.csv")
print(f"{len(homes)} houses on file: {list(homes.columns)}\n")

# The file was built from a known truth, so we can check what the model recovers:
#   ₹3,200 per square foot · ₹250,000 per bedroom · −₹45,000 per year of age

X = homes[["area_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]]
y = homes["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

print("What the model learned:")
for name, coef in zip(X.columns, model.coef_):
    print(f"  {name:<12} {coef:>12,.0f}")
print(f"  {'intercept':<12} {model.intercept_:>12,.0f}")

print("\nRead as sentences (each holds the others constant):")
print(f"  one more square foot  → ₹{model.coef_[0]:>10,.0f}   (same bedrooms, same age)")
print(f"  one more bedroom      → ₹{model.coef_[1]:>10,.0f}   (same area, same age)")
print(f"  one more year of age  → ₹{model.coef_[2]:>10,.0f}   (same area, same bedrooms)")

400 houses on file: ['area_sqft', 'bedrooms', 'age_years', 'price']

What the model learned:
  area_sqft           3,051
  bedrooms          291,399
  age_years         -44,476
  intercept         436,494

Read as sentences (each holds the others constant):
  one more square foot  → ₹     3,051   (same bedrooms, same age)
  one more bedroom      → ₹   291,399   (same area, same age)
  one more year of age  → ₹   -44,476   (same area, same bedrooms)




23.1.2 Demo 7 — why “holding constant” changes the answer

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

alone = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[["bedrooms"]], y_train)
print(f"bedrooms ALONE          : ₹{alone.coef_[0]:>12,.0f} per bedroom")
print(f"bedrooms WITH area, age : ₹{model.coef_[1]:>12,.0f} per bedroom")
print(f"\ncorrelation between area and bedrooms: {X_train['area_sqft'].corr(X_train['bedrooms']):.2f}")

bedrooms ALONE          : ₹   1,492,208 per bedroom
bedrooms WITH area, age : ₹     291,399 per bedroom

correlation between area and bedrooms: 0.95


On its own, a bedroom looks worth far more. That is because bedrooms come attached to floor area, and the single-feature model credits the bedroom with the area’s effect too. Once area is in the model, the bedroom coefficient reports only what a bedroom adds by itself.






Warning⚠️ Highly correlated features make coefficients unreliable



When two features carry nearly the same information — as area and bedrooms do here — the model can split the credit between them almost arbitrarily. The predictions stay fine; the individual coefficients become unstable and should not be quoted as findings. This is called multicollinearity, and Session 8’s heatmap is how you spot it coming.




23.1.3 Demo 8 — adding features one at a time

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error

sets = [["area_sqft"],
        ["area_sqft", "bedrooms"],
        ["area_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]]

print(f"{'features':<40} {'test R²':>9} {'test MAE':>14}")
print("-" * 65)
for cols in sets:
    m = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[cols], y_train)
    pred = m.predict(X_test[cols])
    print(f"{', '.join(cols):<40} {r2_score(y_test, pred):>9.3f} {mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred):>14,.0f}")

features                                   test R²       test MAE
-----------------------------------------------------------------
area_sqft                                    0.868        473,788
area_sqft, bedrooms                          0.866        484,325
area_sqft, bedrooms, age_years               0.971        206,858


Adding bedrooms made the model very slightly worse — 0.868 down to 0.866. Area already carried that information, so the extra column brought no signal and a little noise. Adding age_years improved R² from 0.87 to 0.97 and more than halved the typical error, because age is genuinely new information that area cannot supply.
That is the whole of feature selection in one table: a column earns its place by improving the score on data the model has not seen, not by sounding relevant. Session 6 automates exactly this comparison.

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
24.1 5. The three regression metrics
A prediction is never exactly right. The metric decides how you count the misses.









Metric
What it is
Units
Character




MAE
average size of the error
same as the target
treats all errors evenly


RMSE
square root of the average squared error
same as the target
punishes large errors much harder


R²
share of the variation the model explains
none — a fraction
1.0 perfect, 0 no better than the average




24.1.1 Demo 9 — computed by hand, then by scikit-learn

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

import pandas as pd

preds = pd.read_csv("datasets/predictions_small.csv")
actual, predicted = preds["actual"].values, preds["predicted"].values
errors = predicted - actual

print(f"actual    : {actual.tolist()}")
print(f"predicted : {predicted.tolist()}")
print(f"errors    : {errors.tolist()}")

print(f"\nMAE  = average of |errors|      = {np.abs(errors).mean():.2f}")
print(f"RMSE = √(average of errors²)    = {np.sqrt((errors**2).mean()):.2f}")

ss_res = (errors ** 2).sum()
ss_tot = ((actual - actual.mean()) ** 2).sum()
print(f"R²   = 1 - {ss_res} / {ss_tot:.0f} = {1 - ss_res/ss_tot:.4f}")

print(f"\nscikit-learn agrees: MAE {mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted):.2f}, "
      f"RMSE {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predicted)):.2f}, "
      f"R² {r2_score(actual, predicted):.4f}")

actual    : [100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
predicted : [110, 190, 310, 380, 520]
errors    : [10, -10, 10, -20, 20]

MAE  = average of |errors|      = 14.00
RMSE = √(average of errors²)    = 14.83
R²   = 1 - 1100 / 100000 = 0.9890

scikit-learn agrees: MAE 14.00, RMSE 14.83, R² 0.9890




24.1.2 Demo 10 — why MAE and RMSE disagree, and when it matters

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

import pandas as pd

pat = pd.read_csv("datasets/two_error_patterns.csv")
actual = pat["actual"].values

for name, pred in [("everything off by 20", pat["model_a_spread_out"].values),
                   ("99 perfect, 1 wrong by 2000", pat["model_b_one_disaster"].values)]:
    mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, pred))
    print(f"{name:<30} MAE {mae:7.2f}   RMSE {rmse:7.2f}")

everything off by 20           MAE   20.00   RMSE   20.00
99 perfect, 1 wrong by 2000    MAE   20.00   RMSE  200.00


Both models have the same MAE. RMSE separates them completely, because it squares the errors before averaging — so one enormous mistake counts for far more than a hundred small ones.
Which to report:








If
Use
Because




all errors cost the same
MAE
it is the plain average error, and it is easy to explain


one big error is disastrous — a bridge, a dosage, a delivery promise
RMSE
it makes large errors visible


you are talking to a non-technical audience
MAE
“we are typically off by ₹2 lakh” needs no explanation


you are comparing across different datasets
R²
it has no units





24.1.3 Demo 11 — always compare against a baseline

import numpy as np
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

baseline = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_train, y_train)   # always predicts the average
real     = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

for name, m in [("Baseline (always the mean)", baseline), ("Linear regression", real)]:
    pred = m.predict(X_test)
    print(f"{name:<28} MAE ₹{mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred):>10,.0f}   R² {r2_score(y_test, pred):>7.3f}")

improvement = 1 - mean_absolute_error(y_test, real.predict(X_test)) / \
                  mean_absolute_error(y_test, baseline.predict(X_test))
print(f"\nThe model reduced the typical error by {improvement:.0%} versus guessing the average.")

Baseline (always the mean)   MAE ₹ 1,222,939   R²  -0.011
Linear regression            MAE ₹   206,858   R²   0.971

The model reduced the typical error by 83% versus guessing the average.








Important🔓 R² of 0 means ‘no better than the average’



That is exactly what the baseline scores. R² is defined against that baseline, so a model with R² of 0.02 has essentially learned nothing, and a negative R² means it is worse than always guessing the mean.
Always run the baseline. It converts “R² is 0.62” — which sounds like a number someone could argue about — into “the model cuts the typical error by a third”, which is a business fact.

title: 20  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
24.2 6. Checking the assumptions
Linear regression assumes things about your data. When they are false, the predictions can still work — but the coefficients and confidence in them cannot be trusted.








Assumption
Means
How to check




Linearity
the relationship really is a straight line
residual plot


Constant spread
errors are equally large everywhere
residual plot


Independence
one row’s error tells you nothing about the next
know how the data was collected


No severe multicollinearity
features are not near-copies of each other
correlation heatmap




24.2.1 Demo 12 — the residual plot, and the two shapes that condemn a model

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

import pandas as pd

rs = pd.read_csv("datasets/residual_shapes.csv")
x = rs["x"].values
cases = {
    "Healthy":        rs["healthy"].values,
    "Curved pattern": rs["curved"].values,
    "Fanning out":    rs["fanning_out"].values,
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
for ax, (name, yy) in zip(axes, cases.items()):
    m = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), yy)
    resid = yy - m.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1))
    ax.scatter(m.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1)), resid, s=10, alpha=.6)
    ax.axhline(0, color="red", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel("predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("error")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("A residual plot should look like a shapeless cloud centred on zero.")
print("  A CURVE  → the true relationship is not a straight line; add a squared term")
print("             or use a model that can bend.")
print("  A FAN    → errors grow with the size of the prediction. The model is far less")
print("             reliable for large values than the single R² suggests.")







Figure 24.1: Left: a healthy residual plot — formless cloud around zero. Middle: a curve, so the relationship is not linear. Right: a fan, so error grows with size.





A residual plot should look like a shapeless cloud centred on zero.
  A CURVE  → the true relationship is not a straight line; add a squared term
             or use a model that can bend.
  A FAN    → errors grow with the size of the prediction. The model is far less
             reliable for large values than the single R² suggests.


Session 11 goes further with this. For now: draw the residual plot before you believe the R².


24.2.2 Demo 13 — when the straight line is the wrong shape

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

fuel = pd.read_csv("datasets/fuel_efficiency.csv")
speed, efficiency = fuel["speed_kmh"].values, fuel["efficiency_kmpl"].values
# Efficiency peaks in the middle and falls at both ends — a curve, not a line.

Xs = speed.reshape(-1, 1)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xs, efficiency, test_size=.3, random_state=0)

straight = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
curved   = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)

print(f"straight line       R² = {r2_score(yte, straight.predict(Xte)):.3f}")
print(f"curve (degree 2)    R² = {r2_score(yte, curved.predict(Xte)):.3f}")
print("\nThe straight line explains almost nothing, because efficiency rises then falls.")
print("`PolynomialFeatures(2)` adds a squared term, and the same LinearRegression")
print("then fits a curve — the model is still 'linear' in its coefficients.")

straight line       R² = 0.173
curve (degree 2)    R² = 0.940

The straight line explains almost nothing, because efficiency rises then falls.
`PolynomialFeatures(2)` adds a squared term, and the same LinearRegression
then fits a curve — the model is still 'linear' in its coefficients.

Part

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
22.1 1. Unsupervised learning
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no target column. Nobody has labelled anything; the algorithm has only the features.









Supervised (Session 9)
Unsupervised (this chapter)




Data
X and y
X only


Goal
predict y for new rows
find structure in X


Can you measure accuracy?
yes — compare to the true y
no — there is no true answer


Fails by
predicting badly
producing groups that mean nothing



Three families:








Family
Finds
Covered in




Clustering
groups of similar rows
this chapter


Dimensionality reduction
a smaller set of columns
Session 6 (PCA)


Association rules
things that occur together
Session 16









Tip🧠 Analogy — sorting the laundry



Nobody told you the categories. You tip the basket out and start making piles — darks, whites, towels — because things in a pile resemble each other.
Somebody else would make different piles. By fabric, perhaps, or by owner. Neither is wrong. That is unsupervised learning: several defensible answers, and no marking scheme.
crumbs: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
22.2 2. What clustering is for
Clustering puts rows into groups so that rows in a group are more similar to each other than to rows in other groups.



Use
What the clusters become




Customer segmentation
marketing groups with different offers


Document grouping
topics


Image compression
a small palette of representative colours


Anomaly detection
whatever does not fit any cluster


Exploration
the first look at data nobody has labelled



“Similar” means “close together” — so clustering is a distance calculation, and every warning from Session 5 about scale applies with full force.

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
23.1 3. How K-Means works
K-Means splits data into k groups by repeatedly moving k centre points until they settle.





flowchart TB
    S1["<b>1.</b> Pick k. Place k centres at random"]
    S2["<b>2.</b> Assign every point to its<br/>nearest centre"]
    S3["<b>3.</b> Move each centre to the average<br/>of the points assigned to it"]
    S4{"Did anything<br/>move?"}
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4
    S4 -- yes --> S2
    S4 -- no --> S5["<b>Done.</b> The centres have settled"]






You must choose k yourself. The algorithm cannot tell you how many groups exist — that is the whole difficulty, and Part C is about it.

23.1.1 Demo 1 — watching the centres settle, step by step

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import pandas as pd

points = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values

centres = np.array([[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]])   # deliberately bad starting positions

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.1))
for step, ax in enumerate(axes):
    distances = np.linalg.norm(points[:, None] - centres[None], axis=2)
    labels = distances.argmin(axis=1)                       # step 2: assign
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], c=labels, s=12, cmap="viridis")
    ax.scatter(centres[:, 0], centres[:, 1], c="red", marker="X", s=150, edgecolor="k")
    ax.set_title(f"iteration {step}", fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for j in range(3):                                       # step 3: move
        if (labels == j).any():
            centres[j] = points[labels == j].mean(axis=0)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Started at:", [[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]], "— all three bunched in one corner")
print("Ended at:  ", centres.round(1).tolist())
print("The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7].")







Figure 23.1: Four iterations of K-Means. The crosses are the centres; watch them walk into place.





Started at: [[1.0, 6.0], [2.0, 7.0], [3.0, 6.5]] — all three bunched in one corner
Ended at:   [[1.9, 2.0], [4.1, 7.0], [7.0, 3.0]]
The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7].




23.1.2 Demo 2 — the same thing with scikit-learn

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# A real dataset: 200 mall customers, their annual income and a spending score
# the mall assigned them.
customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={
    "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"})
print(customers.head(3), f"\n\n{len(customers)} customers on file\n")

km = KMeans(n_clusters=5, random_state=0, n_init=10)
customers["cluster"] = km.fit_predict(customers[["income", "spending_score"]])

plt.scatter(customers["income"], customers["spending_score"],
            c=customers["cluster"], cmap="viridis", s=18)
plt.scatter(km.cluster_centers_[:, 0], km.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
            c="red", marker="X", s=220, edgecolor="k", label="centres")
plt.xlabel("Annual income (k$)"); plt.ylabel("Spending score"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(customers.groupby("cluster").agg(
    n=("income", "size"), avg_income=("income", "mean"), avg_spend=("spending_score", "mean")
).round(1))

   CustomerID  Gender  Age  income  spending_score
0           1    Male   19      15              39
1           2    Male   21      15              81
2           3  Female   20      16               6 

200 customers on file









Figure 23.2: Customer segments by income and spending score, with the centres marked.





          n  avg_income  avg_spend
cluster                           
0        81        55.3       49.5
1        39        86.5       82.1
2        35        88.2       17.1
3        23        26.3       20.9
4        22        25.7       79.4


Note n_init=10: K-Means starts from random positions and can settle into a poor arrangement, so it runs ten times from different starts and keeps the best.

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
23.2 4. Scale first — always
K-Means measures straight-line distance. An unscaled column with big numbers decides every cluster on its own.
This is Session 5’s lesson, and clustering is where it does the most damage — because there is no accuracy score to warn you that the answer is wrong.

23.2.1 Demo 3 — real data where the scales genuinely differ
The mall file happens to be convenient: income in thousands (range 122) and spending score out of 100 (range 98) are already on comparable scales, so scaling would change almost nothing. Check before you assume you need it.

import pandas as pd

mall = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={
    "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"})
print("Mall file — the two columns are already comparable:")
for c in ["income", "spending_score"]:
    print(f"  {c:<15} range {mall[c].max() - mall[c].min():>10,.0f}")

Mall file — the two columns are already comparable:
  income          range        122
  spending_score  range         98




23.2.2 Demo 4 — the same file, unscaled versus scaled
A real file where the columns are not comparable. loan_data_10k.csv records income in rupees (hundreds of thousands) next to loan-to-income ratio (a fraction between 0 and 1).

import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

loan = (pd.read_csv("datasets/loan_data_10k.csv")
          .dropna(subset=["person_income", "loan_percent_income"])
          .sample(2_000, random_state=0))
X = loan[["person_income", "loan_percent_income"]]

print("Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable:")
for c in X.columns:
    print(f"  {c:<22} range {X[c].max() - X[c].min():>13,.2f}")

unscaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(X)
scaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax[0].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=unscaled_labels,
              cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[0].set_title("Unscaled — boundaries are vertical")
ax[1].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=scaled_labels,
              cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[1].set_title("Scaled — both columns count")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlabel("Income (₹)"); a.set_ylabel("Loan as a share of income"); a.set_xscale("log")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

agree = pd.crosstab(unscaled_labels, scaled_labels).max(axis=1).sum() / len(X)
print(f"\nUnscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale.")
print(f"The two clusterings agree on only {agree:.0%} of applicants —")
print(f"{1 - agree:.0%} land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled.")

Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable:
  person_income          range    832,912.00
  loan_percent_income    range          0.53








Figure 23.3: Left: unscaled, so income alone decides and the boundaries are vertical. Right: scaled, so both columns count.






Unscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale.
The two clusterings agree on only 57% of applicants —
43% land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled.








Warning⚠️ Unscaled clustering produces confident nonsense



No error is raised. The clusters look tidy, the chart is colourful, and 43% of applicants are in a different group purely because of a unit choice.
Put StandardScaler in front of KMeans unless you have checked that the columns are already comparable — and check by printing the ranges, as the first cell above does.
crumbs: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
24.1 5. The elbow method
Inertia is the total squared distance from every point to its own centre. More clusters always means lower inertia — with one cluster per point it reaches zero — so you cannot simply minimise it.
The elbow method looks for the point where the improvement stops being worth it.

24.1.1 Demo 5 — the elbow on data with a known answer
three_blobs.csv was built from three obvious groups, so this is the easy case: the elbow should land exactly on the true count.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

blobs = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values

print(f"{'k':>3} {'inertia':>10}")
for k in range(1, 7):
    inertia = KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(blobs).inertia_
    print(f"{k:>3} {inertia:>10.1f}")

  k    inertia
  1     1737.7
  2      866.5
  3      121.4
  4      103.6
  5       87.2
  6       73.3


The drop from k=2 to k=3 is huge — 866 down to 121 — and every drop after that is small. With three genuinely separate groups, the elbow is not a judgement call; it is obvious by eye and by number.


24.1.2 Demo 6 — the elbow on real, messier data
Real customers are never this clean. Here the elbow is still visible, but it needs a second look to place.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(customers[["income", "spending_score"]])

ks = range(1, 9)
inertias = [KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(Xs).inertia_ for k in ks]

plt.plot(ks, inertias, "o-")
plt.axvline(5, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("k (number of clusters)"); plt.ylabel("inertia")
plt.title("Where does the line stop dropping steeply?")
plt.show()

print(f"{'k':>3} {'inertia':>10} {'improvement':>13}")
for i, (k, v) in enumerate(zip(ks, inertias)):
    imp = "" if i == 0 else f"{(inertias[i-1]-v)/inertias[i-1]:>12.1%}"
    print(f"{k:>3} {v:>10.1f} {imp:>13}")







Figure 24.1: Inertia falls with every extra cluster. The bend at k=5 is where extra clusters stop paying.





  k    inertia   improvement
  1      400.0              
  2      269.3         32.7%
  3      157.7         41.4%
  4      108.9         30.9%
  5       65.6         39.8%
  6       55.1         15.9%
  7       44.9         18.5%
  8       37.1         17.3%


Read the improvement column: large gains up to k=5, then much smaller ones. That is the elbow — and five is the answer this well-known dataset is famous for.
crumbs: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
24.2 6. The silhouette score
The silhouette score measures, for each point, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the next nearest one. It runs from −1 to +1.







Score
Means




near +1
comfortably inside its own cluster


near 0
on the boundary — could belong to either


negative
closer to a different cluster — probably misassigned



Unlike inertia, it does not automatically improve with more clusters, so you can compare values across different k directly.

24.2.1 Demo 7 — silhouette across k

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

ks = range(2, 9)
scores = [silhouette_score(Xs, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(Xs)) for k in ks]

plt.plot(list(ks), scores, "o-", color="darkgreen")
best = list(ks)[int(np.argmax(scores))]
plt.axvline(best, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("k"); plt.ylabel("silhouette score"); plt.title("Higher is better")
plt.show()

for k, s in zip(ks, scores):
    print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {s:.3f}{'   ← best' if k == best else ''}")







Figure 24.2: Silhouette by k. Unlike inertia, higher is genuinely better, so the peak is the answer.





k = 2: silhouette 0.286
k = 3: silhouette 0.467
k = 4: silhouette 0.494
k = 5: silhouette 0.555   ← best
k = 6: silhouette 0.538
k = 7: silhouette 0.526
k = 8: silhouette 0.457


Both methods point at the same answer here. They do not always.


24.2.2 Demo 8 — when the silhouette score is wrong

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Two interleaved crescents. The true structure is obviously 2 groups.
mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv")
moons = mo[["x", "y"]].values
true_labels = mo["true_group"].values

for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons)
    print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {silhouette_score(moons, labels):.3f}")

agree = (KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons) == true_labels)
print(f"\nAt k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for "
      f"{max(agree.mean(), 1-agree.mean()):.0%} of points.")
print("The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong")
print("place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not")
print("mean a good clustering.")

k = 2: silhouette 0.489
k = 3: silhouette 0.428
k = 4: silhouette 0.461

At k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for 76% of points.
The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong
place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not
mean a good clustering.








Warning⚠️ Clustering always returns clusters



Ask K-Means for four groups in pure random noise and you will get four groups, each with a centre and a colour, and a chart that looks meaningful.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

noise = pd.read_csv("datasets/random_noise.csv")[["x", "y"]].values   # no structure at all
for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    print(f"k = {k} on pure noise: silhouette {silhouette_score(noise, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(noise)):.3f}")

k = 2 on pure noise: silhouette 0.314
k = 3 on pure noise: silhouette 0.326
k = 4 on pure noise: silhouette 0.321


Those are not zero. The elbow and the silhouette are evidence, not proof. The real test is whether the clusters mean something to somebody who knows the business.

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
section: 24.3 7. Profiling: turning clusters into an answer
text:
24.3 7. Profiling: turning clusters into an answer
A cluster number is not a deliverable. cluster = 2 means nothing to a marketing team. The deliverable is a description.

24.3.1 Demo 9 — the profile table, on its own
Before naming anything, the basic move is just a groupby on the cluster label — one row of summary numbers per cluster.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

blobs = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")
blobs["cluster"] = KMeans(3, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(blobs[["x", "y"]])

profile = blobs.groupby("cluster").agg(
    n=("x", "size"), mean_x=("x", "mean"), mean_y=("y", "mean")
).round(2)
print(profile)

          n  mean_x  mean_y
cluster                    
0        60    6.98    2.96
1        60    4.06    7.00
2        60    1.93    2.00


Three clusters, three rows, and already a description of sorts — cluster 2 sits near (2, 2), cluster 1 near (4, 7), cluster 0 near (7, 3). The mall data below adds the step this one skips: turning those numbers into words a non-technical reader can act on.


24.3.2 Demo 10 — from cluster numbers to named segments

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X = customers[["income", "spending_score"]]
customers["segment"] = KMeans(5, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(
    StandardScaler().fit_transform(X))

profile = customers.groupby("segment").agg(
    customers=("income", "size"),
    median_income=("income", "median"),
    median_spend=("spending_score", "median"),
).round(0)
profile["share"] = (profile["customers"] / len(customers) * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
print(profile)

print("\nNow name them, and say what to do:")
overall_income = customers["income"].median()
overall_spend = customers["spending_score"].median()
for seg, row in profile.iterrows():
    rich = "high" if row["median_income"] > overall_income else "modest"
    spends = "high" if row["median_spend"] > overall_spend else "low"
    name = {("high", "high"): "Best customers — reward and retain",
            ("high", "low"):  "Untapped — money, but not spending here",
            ("modest", "low"): "Budget-conscious — low priority",
            ("modest", "high"): "Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully"}[(rich, spends)]
    print(f"  Segment {seg}: {name:<44} ({row['share']:>5} of customers, "
          f"${row['median_income']:,.0f}k income)")

         customers  median_income  median_spend  share
segment                                               
0               81           54.0          50.0  40.5%
1               39           79.0          83.0  19.5%
2               35           85.0          16.0  17.5%
3               23           25.0          17.0  11.5%
4               22           24.0          77.0  11.0%

Now name them, and say what to do:
  Segment 0: Budget-conscious — low priority              (40.5% of customers, $54k income)
  Segment 1: Best customers — reward and retain           (19.5% of customers, $79k income)
  Segment 2: Untapped — money, but not spending here      (17.5% of customers, $85k income)
  Segment 3: Budget-conscious — low priority              (11.5% of customers, $25k income)
  Segment 4: Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully     (11.0% of customers, $24k income)


That last block is the actual output of a clustering project. “Segment 1” became “high income, not spending — worth a targeted offer”, which somebody can act on tomorrow.
crumbs: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
25.1 8. Hierarchical clustering
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree. It starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest, until everything is one cluster. You then cut the tree wherever you like.
Its advantage over K-Means: you do not have to choose k in advance. You build the tree once and read off any number of clusters from it.

25.1.1 Demo 11 — building the tree once, cutting it several ways

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster

blobs = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values
Z = linkage(blobs, method="ward")   # build the tree ONCE

for cut in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = fcluster(Z, cut, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"cutting for {cut} clusters → sizes {np.bincount(labels)[1:].tolist()}")

cutting for 2 clusters → sizes [60, 120]
cutting for 3 clusters → sizes [60, 60, 60]
cutting for 4 clusters → sizes [60, 60, 13, 47]


One call to linkage and three different answers, just by cutting the same tree at a different height. Cutting for 3 recovers the true groups exactly — 60, 60, 60 — because three_blobs.csv really does have three well-separated clusters.


25.1.2 Demo 12 — the dendrogram, on messier real data

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sample = customers[["income", "spending_score"]].sample(40, random_state=1)
Z = linkage(StandardScaler().fit_transform(sample), method="ward")

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.4))
dendrogram(Z, no_labels=True)
plt.axhline(6, color="red", ls="--")
plt.ylabel("distance at which clusters merged")
plt.title("Cut the tree where the vertical lines are longest")
plt.show()

for cut in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = fcluster(Z, cut, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"cutting for {cut} clusters → sizes {np.bincount(labels)[1:].tolist()}")







Figure 25.1: A dendrogram. Cutting across at a height gives that many clusters — the long vertical gap suggests where.





cutting for 2 clusters → sizes [9, 31]
cutting for 3 clusters → sizes [9, 5, 26]
cutting for 4 clusters → sizes [9, 5, 5, 21]
crumbs: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 21  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
25.2 9. DBSCAN
DBSCAN groups points that are packed closely together and labels everything else as noise. It has two strengths K-Means does not:

clusters can be any shape, not just round blobs
points that belong to no cluster are marked as noise rather than forced into one

You do not give it k. You give it eps (how close counts as “near”) and min_samples (how many neighbours make a dense region).

25.2.1 Demo 13 — the crescents, where K-Means could not win

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN

mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv")
moons, truth = mo[["x", "y"]].values, mo["true_group"].values

km_labels = KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons)
db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit_predict(moons)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax[0].scatter(*moons.T, c=truth, cmap="viridis", s=10);      ax[0].set_title("The truth")
ax[1].scatter(*moons.T, c=km_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10);  ax[1].set_title("K-Means")
ax[2].scatter(*moons.T, c=db_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10);  ax[2].set_title("DBSCAN")
for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

km_acc = max((km_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (km_labels == truth).mean())
db_acc = max((db_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (db_labels == truth).mean())
print(f"K-Means matches the true crescents: {km_acc:.0%}")
print(f"DBSCAN  matches the true crescents: {db_acc:.0%}")
print(f"DBSCAN labelled {(db_labels == -1).sum()} points as noise (label -1)")







Figure 25.2: K-Means cuts the crescents with a straight line. DBSCAN follows their shape.





K-Means matches the true crescents: 76%
DBSCAN  matches the true crescents: 100%
DBSCAN labelled 0 points as noise (label -1)




25.2.2 Demo 14 — choosing between the three

print(f"{'':<22} {'K-Means':<22} {'Hierarchical':<22} {'DBSCAN'}")
rows = [
    ("must choose k?",     "yes",                 "no — cut the tree",   "no"),
    ("cluster shapes",     "round blobs only",    "flexible",            "any shape"),
    ("handles noise",      "no — forces a group", "no",                  "yes, explicitly"),
    ("speed on big data",  "fast",                "slow (n² memory)",    "medium"),
    ("clusters of very different density", "poor", "fair",               "poor"),
    ("main use",           "the default first try","exploring structure","odd shapes, outliers"),
]
for label, a, b, c in rows:
    print(f"{label:<22} {a:<22} {b:<22} {c}")

                       K-Means                Hierarchical           DBSCAN
must choose k?         yes                    no — cut the tree      no
cluster shapes         round blobs only       flexible               any shape
handles noise          no — forces a group    no                     yes, explicitly
speed on big data      fast                   slow (n² memory)       medium
clusters of very different density poor                   fair                   poor
main use               the default first try  exploring structure    odd shapes, outliers

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
22.1 🎯 Learning outcomes
By the end of this chapter you can:

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
Recognise overfitting and underfitting from training and test scores.
Explain the bias–variance trade-off in plain words.
Run k-fold cross-validation and report a score with its spread.
Choose between holdout, k-fold, stratified k-fold, leave-one-out and bootstrapping.
Diagnose a model from its residual plot and its error distribution.
Tune hyperparameters with grid search without touching the test set.
Explain why tuning on the test set invalidates the result.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
22.2 How this chapter is organised



Part
Question it answers




A — The two failures
What are the ways a model goes wrong?


B — Validation strategies
How do I get a score I can trust?


C — Evaluating with pictures
What does the score not tell me?


D — Tuning
How do I improve it without cheating?

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
23.1 1. Overfitting and underfitting
A model can fail in two opposite directions.









Underfitting
Overfitting




The model is
too simple
too complex


Training score
poor
excellent


Test score
poor
poor


It has
missed the pattern
memorised the noise


Fix by
adding features, using a richer model
simplifying, adding data, regularising



The diagnosis is the gap. Poor on both means underfitting. Excellent on training and poor on test means overfitting.






Tip🧠 Analogy — three students revising




The underfitting student skimmed one page. They do badly on the practice papers and badly in the exam.
The overfitting student memorised every practice paper word for word. Perfect on practice, lost in the exam when the questions are worded differently.
The good student learned the method. Slightly imperfect on practice, and fine in the exam.

Only the exam tells them apart — which is why the test set must stay sealed.



23.1.1 Demo 1 — watching a model overfit, in one table

import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

import pandas as pd

line = pd.read_csv("datasets/noisy_line.csv")   # 40 points on a noisy straight line
x, y = line["x"].values, line["y"].values

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(x.reshape(-1, 1), y, test_size=.35, random_state=0)

print(f"{'model':<14} {'train R²':>9} {'test R²':>11}   verdict")
print("-" * 52)
for degree in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 16]:
    # StandardScaler between the two steps keeps high powers numerically stable
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    tr, te = r2_score(ytr, m.predict(Xtr)), r2_score(yte, m.predict(Xte))
    verdict = "OVERFITTING" if tr - te > 0.2 else "reasonable"
    print(f"degree {degree:<7} {tr:>9.3f} {te:>11.3f}   {verdict}")

model           train R²     test R²   verdict
----------------------------------------------------
degree 1           0.640       0.767   reasonable
degree 2           0.643       0.746   reasonable
degree 3           0.647       0.717   reasonable
degree 5           0.666       0.796   reasonable
degree 8           0.707      -2.975   OVERFITTING
degree 12          0.722     -44.941   OVERFITTING
degree 16          0.717    -187.128   OVERFITTING


Watch the two columns separate. Training R² climbs steadily as the model is given more freedom — it can always bend closer to points it has already seen. The test score peaks around degree 5 and then falls off a cliff: −45 at degree 12, −187 at degree 16.
A negative R² means worse than always guessing the average. The degree-16 model fits its training data better than any other model in the table and is, on unseen data, far worse than useless.


23.1.2 Demo 2 — the same thing as a picture

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
for ax, degree in zip(axes, [1, 3, 14]):
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    ax.scatter(Xtr, ytr, s=18, label="training")
    ax.scatter(Xte, yte, s=18, color="orange", label="test")
    ax.plot(grid, m.predict(grid), "r-", lw=1.8)
    ax.set_ylim(y.min()-6, y.max()+6)
    ax.set_title(f"degree {degree}", fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Degree 14 passes almost exactly through the blue training points — and swings")
print("wildly between them, which is where the orange test points live.")







Figure 23.1: Degree 1 misses the pattern. Degree 14 passes through every training point and is useless between them.





Degree 14 passes almost exactly through the blue training points — and swings
wildly between them, which is where the orange test points live.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
23.2 2. Bias and variance
These are the technical names for the two failures.








Term
Means
Shows up as




Bias
error from wrong assumptions — the model is too simple to represent the truth
underfitting


Variance
error from sensitivity to the particular training data
overfitting



The trade-off: making a model more flexible reduces bias and increases variance. There is a middle point, and finding it is what the rest of this chapter is for.

23.2.1 Demo 3 — variance made visible

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

import pandas as pd

samples = pd.read_csv("datasets/repeated_samples.csv")   # six draws from the same truth
grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 200).reshape(-1, 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.3))
for degree, a in zip([1, 12], ax):
    for sample_id, g in samples.groupby("sample"):
        xs, ys = g["x"].values, g["y"].values
        m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression()).fit(xs.reshape(-1,1), ys)
        a.plot(grid, m.predict(grid), lw=1.2, alpha=.8)
    a.set_ylim(-10, 30); a.set_title(f"degree {degree}: {'low' if degree==1 else 'high'} variance")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Left: six nearly identical lines — low variance, the model is stable.")
print("Right: six wildly different curves from the same underlying truth —")
print("       high variance. Which one you get depends on which rows you happened to draw.")







Figure 23.2: The same model fitted to six different samples from the same source. The flexible model changes shape wildly; the simple one barely moves.





Left: six nearly identical lines — low variance, the model is stable.
Right: six wildly different curves from the same underlying truth —
       high variance. Which one you get depends on which rows you happened to draw.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
section: 24.1 3. Why one split is not enough
text:
24.1 3. Why one split is not enough
A single train–test split gives you one number, and that number depends on which rows happened to land in the test set.

24.1.1 Demo 4 — the same model, twenty different scores

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

feats = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_features.csv")
X = feats[["f1", "f2", "f3"]].values
y = feats["target"].values

scores = []
for seed in range(20):
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=seed)
    scores.append(r2_score(yte, LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)))

scores = np.array(scores)
print(f"lowest  R² : {scores.min():.3f}")
print(f"highest R² : {scores.max():.3f}")
print(f"spread     : {scores.max()-scores.min():.3f}")
print(f"average    : {scores.mean():.3f}  (± {scores.std():.3f})")
print("\nSame model, same data, same code. Only the random seed changed.")

lowest  R² : 0.556
highest R² : 0.795
spread     : 0.239
average    : 0.695  (± 0.063)

Same model, same data, same code. Only the random seed changed.








Warning⚠️ Report a range, not a point



If your model scores 0.71 and a colleague’s scores 0.74, and single splits vary by 0.15, you have not shown that yours is worse. You have shown two draws from overlapping ranges.
Any comparison of two models must use the same folds and account for the spread.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
24.2 4. K-fold cross-validation
Cross-validation splits the data into k parts, then trains k times — each time holding out a different part for testing. Every row is used for testing exactly once.





flowchart TB
    D["all training data, split into 5 folds"]
    D --> R1["run 1: test on fold 1, train on 2,3,4,5"]
    D --> R2["run 2: test on fold 2, train on 1,3,4,5"]
    D --> R3["run 3: test on fold 3, train on 1,2,4,5"]
    D --> R4["run 4: test on fold 4, train on 1,2,3,5"]
    D --> R5["run 5: test on fold 5, train on 1,2,3,4"]
    R1 --> A["average the 5 scores<br/><b>and report the spread</b>"]
    R2 --> A
    R3 --> A
    R4 --> A
    R5 --> A







24.2.1 Demo 5 — cross-validation, fold by fold

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold

cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
fold_scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=cv, scoring="r2")

for i, s in enumerate(fold_scores, 1):
    print(f"  fold {i}: R² = {s:.3f}")
print(f"\nreport this: R² = {fold_scores.mean():.3f} ± {fold_scores.std():.3f}")
print(f"a single split could have given you anything from {fold_scores.min():.3f} "
      f"to {fold_scores.max():.3f}")

  fold 1: R² = 0.703
  fold 2: R² = 0.802
  fold 3: R² = 0.729
  fold 4: R² = 0.732
  fold 5: R² = 0.656

report this: R² = 0.724 ± 0.047
a single split could have given you anything from 0.656 to 0.802

text:
24.3 5. Choosing a validation strategy

print(f"{'strategy':<24} {'how it works':<44} {'use when'}")
print("-" * 108)
rows = [
    ("Holdout",           "one split, e.g. 80/20",                      "data is huge; you need a quick answer"),
    ("K-fold",            "k splits, every row tested once",            "the default"),
    ("Stratified k-fold", "k-fold keeping class proportions",           "classification, especially imbalanced"),
    ("Leave-one-out",     "k = number of rows",                         "very small datasets; expensive"),
    ("Bootstrapping",     "sample with replacement, many times",        "you want a confidence interval"),
    ("Time-series split", "always train on the past, test on the future","the rows are ordered in time"),
]
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r[0]:<24} {r[1]:<44} {r[2]}")

strategy                 how it works                                 use when
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Holdout                  one split, e.g. 80/20                        data is huge; you need a quick answer
K-fold                   k splits, every row tested once              the default
Stratified k-fold        k-fold keeping class proportions             classification, especially imbalanced
Leave-one-out            k = number of rows                           very small datasets; expensive
Bootstrapping            sample with replacement, many times          you want a confidence interval
Time-series split        always train on the past, test on the future the rows are ordered in time








Warning⚠️ Never shuffle time-ordered data



Ordinary k-fold shuffles rows, so a model can be trained on next month and tested on last month. It will look excellent and be worthless, because in production the future is not available. For anything with a time order, use TimeSeriesSplit.



24.3.1 Demo 6 — bootstrapping for a confidence interval

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(54)
boot_scores = []
for _ in range(500):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(X), len(X))               # sample rows WITH replacement
    oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), idx)          # rows not drawn = the test set
    if len(oob) < 5:
        continue
    m = LinearRegression().fit(X[idx], y[idx])
    boot_scores.append(r2_score(y[oob], m.predict(X[oob])))

lo, hi = np.percentile(boot_scores, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"bootstrap estimate of R²: {np.mean(boot_scores):.3f}")
print(f"95% confidence interval : {lo:.3f} to {hi:.3f}")
print(f"\nBased on {len(boot_scores)} resamples. Quote the interval, not the point.")

bootstrap estimate of R²: 0.705
95% confidence interval : 0.562 to 0.802

Based on 500 resamples. Quote the interval, not the point.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
section: 25.1 6. What a score cannot tell you
text:
25.1 6. What a score cannot tell you
A single number compresses every mistake into one figure, and hides where the mistakes are. Two models with identical R² can be wrong in completely different ways.

25.1.1 Demo 7 — the residual plot

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

import pandas as pd

rc = pd.read_csv("datasets/residual_cases.csv")
xs = rc["x"].values
cases = {
    "Healthy":         rc["healthy"].values,
    "Missing a curve": rc["curved"].values,
    "Growing error":   rc["growing_error"].values,
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
for ax, (name, yy) in zip(axes, cases.items()):
    m = LinearRegression().fit(xs.reshape(-1,1), yy)
    pred = m.predict(xs.reshape(-1,1))
    ax.scatter(pred, yy - pred, s=9, alpha=.6)
    ax.axhline(0, color="red", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nR² = {m.score(xs.reshape(-1,1), yy):.3f}", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("residual")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("All three have a respectable R². Only the first is a model you should ship.")
print("  curve  → the relationship is not linear; the model is systematically wrong")
print("           at both ends and systematically right in the middle")
print("  fan    → the model is reliable for small predictions and unreliable for large")
print("           ones. A single R² averages those two very different situations.")







Figure 25.1: Predicted versus residual. A healthy model shows a shapeless band around zero.





All three have a respectable R². Only the first is a model you should ship.
  curve  → the relationship is not linear; the model is systematically wrong
           at both ends and systematically right in the middle
  fan    → the model is reliable for small predictions and unreliable for large
           ones. A single R² averages those two very different situations.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
25.2 7. The distribution of the errors
Plotting the errors themselves shows whether the model is biased and how bad the worst cases are.

25.2.1 Demo 8 — the error distribution, and what it reveals

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

shapes = pd.read_csv("datasets/error_shapes.csv")
Xa = shapes[["f1", "f2"]].values
good_y = shapes["target_normal"].values
skew_y = shapes["target_heavy"].values     # heavy tails: rare, very large errors

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
for a, (name, yy) in zip(ax, [("Healthy errors", good_y), ("Heavy-tailed errors", skew_y)]):
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xa, yy, test_size=.3, random_state=0)
    err = yte - LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)
    a.hist(err, bins=40); a.axvline(0, color="red")
    a.set_title(f"{name}\nmean error {err.mean():+.2f}, worst {np.abs(err).max():.1f}", fontsize=9)
    a.set_xlabel("error")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Both models have a mean error near zero — they are unbiased on average.")
print("The right-hand one still has occasional predictions that are badly wrong.")
print("If a single bad prediction is expensive, the average was never the right measure.")







Figure 25.2: Left: errors centred on zero and symmetric — healthy. Right: a long tail, so a few predictions are badly wrong.





Both models have a mean error near zero — they are unbiased on average.
The right-hand one still has occasional predictions that are badly wrong.
If a single bad prediction is expensive, the average was never the right measure.




25.2.2 Demo 9 — predicted versus actual

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xa, good_y, test_size=.3, random_state=0)
pred = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)

plt.scatter(yte, pred, s=12, alpha=.6)
lims = [min(yte.min(), pred.min()), max(yte.max(), pred.max())]
plt.plot(lims, lims, "r--", lw=1.5, label="perfect prediction")
plt.xlabel("actual"); plt.ylabel("predicted"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print("Points above the line: the model predicted too high. Below: too low.")
print("A systematic tilt away from the diagonal means the model is biased at one end.")







Figure 25.3: Predicted against actual. Perfect predictions lie on the diagonal.





Points above the line: the model predicted too high. Below: too low.
A systematic tilt away from the diagonal means the model is biased at one end.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
25.3 8. Learning curves
A learning curve shows the score as training data increases. It tells you what to do next.

25.3.1 Demo 10 — “get more data” or “get a better model”?

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

curved = pd.read_csv("datasets/curved_truth.csv")      # the truth here is a curve
Xb = curved[["f1", "f2"]].values
yb = curved["target"].values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3))
for a, (name, model) in zip(ax, [("Too simple (linear)", LinearRegression()),
                                 ("Flexible (deep tree)", DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0))]):
    sizes, train_s, val_s = learning_curve(model, Xb, yb, cv=5,
                                           train_sizes=np.linspace(.1, 1, 8), scoring="r2")
    a.plot(sizes, train_s.mean(1), "o-", label="training score")
    a.plot(sizes, val_s.mean(1), "o-", label="validation score")
    a.set_title(name, fontsize=10); a.set_xlabel("training rows"); a.set_ylim(-.1, 1.05)
    a.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("LEFT — both curves flat and low, sitting on top of each other:")
print("       the model is too simple. More data changes nothing. Change the model.")
print("RIGHT — a gap between the curves that is still narrowing:")
print("       the model is learning. More data would still help.")







Figure 25.4: Left: the curves converge at a poor score — more data will not help. Right: a gap that is still closing — more data will help.





LEFT — both curves flat and low, sitting on top of each other:
       the model is too simple. More data changes nothing. Change the model.
RIGHT — a gap between the curves that is still narrowing:
       the model is learning. More data would still help.

title: 22  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
26.1 9. Hyperparameters
A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training — the depth of a tree, the k in k-Nearest Neighbours, the strength of a regularisation penalty. The model learns its coefficients; it does not learn these.








Method
How it searches
Use when




Grid search
every combination you list
few settings, small ranges


Random search
random combinations, a fixed budget
many settings — usually beats grid for the same cost


Bayesian optimisation
uses past results to choose what to try next
training is expensive




26.1.1 Demo 11 — grid search, done correctly

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

grid = GridSearchCV(
    DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0),
    param_grid={"max_depth": [2, 3, 5, 8, 12, None],
                "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20]},
    cv=5, scoring="r2",
)
grid.fit(Xtr, ytr)          # note: only the TRAINING data goes in here

print(f"combinations tried : {len(grid.cv_results_['params'])}")
print(f"best settings      : {grid.best_params_}")
print(f"best CV score      : {grid.best_score_:.3f}   (measured on the training folds)")
print(f"score on the sealed test set: {r2_score(yte, grid.predict(Xte)):.3f}")

combinations tried : 18
best settings      : {'max_depth': 12, 'min_samples_leaf': 1}
best CV score      : 0.944   (measured on the training folds)
score on the sealed test set: 0.945


The test set was used exactly once, at the very end. The search compared 18 combinations using cross-validation inside the training data.


26.1.2 Demo 12 — what tuning on the test set does
The damage from peeking is selection bias: when you try many candidates and keep the one that scored highest, the score you kept is partly a measure of luck. Here the signal is genuinely weak, so the candidates are nearly equivalent and “best” is mostly noise — which is exactly the situation where peeking hurts most.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

weak = pd.read_csv("datasets/weak_signal.csv")   # one real driver, buried in noise
Xw = weak[[f"f{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]].values
yw = weak["target"].values

Xtr, Xtmp, ytr, ytmp = train_test_split(Xw, yw, test_size=.4, random_state=0)
Xpeek, Xfresh, ypeek, yfresh = train_test_split(Xtmp, ytmp, test_size=.5, random_state=1)

candidates = [(d, leaf) for d in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, None]
                        for leaf in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80]]

def score_on(Xset, yset, depth, leaf):
    m = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, min_samples_leaf=leaf, random_state=0)
    return r2_score(yset, m.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xset))

peeked = {c: score_on(Xpeek, ypeek, *c) for c in candidates}
best = max(peeked, key=peeked.get)

print(f"settings tried            : {len(candidates)}")
print(f"best score while peeking  : {peeked[best]:+.3f}   (max_depth={best[0]}, min_samples_leaf={best[1]})")
print(f"that same model, fresh data: {score_on(Xfresh, yfresh, *best):+.3f}")
print(f"\nflattery                  : {peeked[best] - score_on(Xfresh, yfresh, *best):+.3f}")
print(f"average candidate, peek set : {np.mean(list(peeked.values())):+.3f}")

settings tried            : 56
best score while peeking  : +0.084   (max_depth=2, min_samples_leaf=80)
that same model, fresh data: -0.204

flattery                  : +0.288
average candidate, peek set : -0.189


The reported figure was positive. The truth was negative. Nothing about that model was good — it was simply the luckiest of 56 draws against one small set of rows, and the score that made it look best was the part that would not repeat.
Note that the average candidate scored badly on the peek set too. The problem is not that the models were good and got worse; it is that taking the maximum over many noisy measurements returns an inflated measurement.






Important🔓 The test set is spent after one use



Every time you look at the test score and change something because of it, you leak a little information into your choices. Do it twenty times and the test set has quietly become a second training set.
The discipline:

Split off the test set and do not touch it
Do all tuning with cross-validation on the training data
Look at the test set once, at the very end, and report what it says
If you then change the model, you need a fresh test set





26.1.3 Demo 13 — the whole evaluation, as one report

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

for name, model in [("Baseline (mean)", DummyRegressor()),
                    ("Linear regression", LinearRegression()),
                    ("Random forest", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=120, random_state=0))]:
    folds = cross_val_score(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="r2")
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    pred = model.predict(Xte)
    print(f"{name:<20} CV R² {folds.mean():>6.3f} ± {folds.std():.3f}   "
          f"test R² {r2_score(yte, pred):>6.3f}   test MAE {mean_absolute_error(yte, pred):>5.2f}")

print("\nThe forest wins, and the ± tells you the win is larger than the fold-to-fold noise.")

Baseline (mean)      CV R² -0.010 ± 0.009   test R² -0.000   test MAE  3.02
Linear regression    CV R²  0.375 ± 0.053   test R²  0.514   test MAE  2.06
Random forest        CV R²  0.972 ± 0.006   test R²  0.969   test MAE  0.47

The forest wins, and the ± tells you the win is larger than the fold-to-fold noise.

title: 23  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
section: 24.1 1. Why a trained model has to be saved
text:
24.1 1. Why a trained model has to be saved
Training happens once; predicting happens thousands of times. Retraining a model every time somebody asks a question would be slow, expensive, and would give slightly different answers each run.
So the trained model is written to a file. That file contains the learned numbers — coefficients, tree splits, the scaler’s mean — and can be loaded in milliseconds.






Tip🧠 Analogy — the recipe and the cooking



Working out a recipe takes weeks of experimenting. Cooking from it takes twenty minutes.
Training is developing the recipe. Saving is writing it down. Prediction is cooking. You do not redevelop the recipe every time somebody orders dinner.
crumbs: 23  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment

title: 23  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
section: 24.2 2. Save the pipeline, not the model
text:
24.2 2. Save the pipeline, not the model
This is the mistake that costs the most and announces itself the least.
A trained LinearRegression knows its coefficients. It does not know that its inputs were scaled before training. Feed it raw, unscaled numbers and it will apply coefficients meant for scaled ones — and return a number, confidently, with no error.

24.2.1 Demo 1 — the silent failure, measured

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

homes = pd.read_csv("datasets/house_prices_simple.csv")
print(f"{len(homes)} houses on file: {list(homes.columns)}\n")

X = homes[["area_sqft", "age_years"]]
y = homes["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.2, random_state=0)

# Train with scaling, as Session 5 taught.
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)
model = LinearRegression().fit(scaler.transform(X_train), y_train)

new_house = pd.DataFrame([{"area_sqft": 1500, "age_years": 5}])

right = model.predict(scaler.transform(new_house))[0]     # scaled, as trained
wrong = model.predict(new_house)[0]                       # raw — the bug

print(f"Correct  (scaled input) : ₹{right:>15,.0f}")
print(f"Bug      (raw input)    : ₹{wrong:>15,.0f}")
print(f"\nNo error was raised. The wrong answer is off by ₹{abs(right-wrong):,.0f}.")

500 houses on file: ['area_sqft', 'age_years', 'price']

Correct  (scaled input) : ₹      4,994,176
Bug      (raw input)    : ₹  1,694,069,949

No error was raised. The wrong answer is off by ₹1,689,075,773.


Both lines ran without complaint. In a web app, the second would be shown to a user as a house valuation.


24.2.2 Demo 2 — the fix: one object that carries everything

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LinearRegression()),
]).fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Pipeline on raw input   : ₹{pipeline.predict(new_house)[0]:>15,.0f}")
print(f"Correct answer from above: ₹{right:>15,.0f}")
print("\nThe pipeline takes RAW input and scales it internally. There is no way")
print("to forget the scaler, because the scaler is inside the thing you saved.")

Pipeline on raw input   : ₹      4,994,176
Correct answer from above: ₹      4,994,176

The pipeline takes RAW input and scales it internally. There is no way
to forget the scaler, because the scaler is inside the thing you saved.

title: 23  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
text:
24.3 3. Saving and loading
joblib writes a fitted Python object to a file and reads it back. It is preferred over pickle for scikit-learn because it stores large numeric arrays more efficiently.

24.3.1 Demo 3 — a full save-and-reload round trip

import joblib, tempfile, os
import numpy as np

folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path = os.path.join(folder, "house_price_pipeline.joblib")

joblib.dump(pipeline, path)
print(f"saved to {os.path.basename(path)}  ({os.path.getsize(path):,} bytes)")

loaded = joblib.load(path)
print(f"loaded back: {type(loaded).__name__} with steps {[n for n, _ in loaded.steps]}")

before = pipeline.predict(X_test)
after   = loaded.predict(X_test)
print(f"\npredictions identical after reload: {np.allclose(before, after)}")
print(f"largest difference: {np.abs(before - after).max():.10f}")

saved to house_price_pipeline.joblib  (1,361 bytes)
loaded back: Pipeline with steps ['scale', 'model']

predictions identical after reload: True
largest difference: 0.0000000000




24.3.2 Demo 4 — save everything needed to reproduce the model

import joblib, sklearn, os, json
from datetime import date
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

bundle = {
    "pipeline": pipeline,
    "feature_names": list(X.columns),           # so the app builds rows in the right order
    "target": "price",
    "trained_on": str(date.today()),
    "n_training_rows": len(X_train),
    "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__,
    "test_mae": float(mean_absolute_error(y_test, pipeline.predict(X_test))),
    "test_r2": float(r2_score(y_test, pipeline.predict(X_test))),
}

bundle_path = os.path.join(folder, "model_bundle.joblib")
joblib.dump(bundle, bundle_path)

back = joblib.load(bundle_path)
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in back.items() if k != "pipeline"}, indent=2))

{
  "feature_names": [
    "area_sqft",
    "age_years"
  ],
  "target": "price",
  "trained_on": "2026-09-24",
  "n_training_rows": 400,
  "sklearn_version": "1.9.0",
  "test_mae": 169824.38561731137,
  "test_r2": 0.9679916797170471
}


Everything except the pipeline itself is metadata, and every field earns its place:







Field
Answers




feature_names
what order do the columns go in?


sklearn_version
why does this behave differently now?


test_mae, test_r2
is the live model still as good as when we shipped it?


trained_on
how stale is this?









Warning⚠️ A saved model is tied to its library version



A pipeline saved under scikit-learn 1.3 and loaded under 1.5 may warn, may behave differently, or may refuse to load. Pin your versions in requirements.txt and record the version in the bundle so the mismatch is diagnosable rather than mysterious.



print("requirements.txt should pin exactly what trained the model, for example:")
print(f"  scikit-learn=={sklearn.__version__}")
print(f"  pandas=={pd.__version__}")
print(f"  numpy=={np.__version__}")

requirements.txt should pin exactly what trained the model, for example:
  scikit-learn==1.9.0
  pandas==3.0.5
  numpy==2.4.6
