text:
30.1 8. Why a scatter plot of ten million points is useless
Draw ten million dots and you get a solid rectangle. The dots overlap — a phenomenon called overplotting — and where one dot sits, a thousand look identical.

30.1.1 Demo 11 — the same data, two sizes

import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pts = pd.read_csv("datasets/overplot_points.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.2))
ax[0].scatter(pts["x"][:500], pts["y"][:500], s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[0].set_title("500 points — still readable", fontsize=9)
ax[1].scatter(pts["x"][:50_000], pts["y"][:50_000], s=1, alpha=.4)
ax[1].set_title("50,000 points — already a blob", fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(pts):,} points available in the file; the full set makes it worse still.")







Figure 30.1: The same underlying data at 500 points and at 50,000 points. Overplotting is not a property of the data — it is what happens once there are too many dots for the pixels available.





200,000 points available in the file; the full set makes it worse still.




30.1.2 Demo 12 — overplotting, and three fixes

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import pandas as pd

pts = pd.read_csv("datasets/overplot_points.csv")
x, y = pts["x"].values, pts["y"].values
n = len(pts)
print(f"{n:,} points loaded from datasets/overplot_points.csv\n")

rng = np.random.default_rng(91)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.1))

ax[0].scatter(x, y, s=1, alpha=.5)
ax[0].set_title("raw scatter\n(a blob)", fontsize=9)

idx = rng.choice(n, 4_000, replace=False)
ax[1].scatter(x[idx], y[idx], s=4, alpha=.5)
ax[1].set_title("random sample\nof 4,000", fontsize=9)

ax[2].hexbin(x, y, gridsize=45, cmap="viridis")
ax[2].set_title("hexbin\n(count per cell)", fontsize=9)

ax[3].hist2d(x, y, bins=90, cmap="viridis")
ax[3].set_title("2-D histogram", fontsize=9)

for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{n:,} points plotted four ways.")
print("The raw scatter hides that there are TWO groups. The other three show it.")

200,000 points loaded from datasets/overplot_points.csv

30.2 9. Aggregate before you plot
The most effective technique is to never send the raw rows to the chart at all. Summarise in the database, plot the summary.

30.2.1 Demo 13 — the idea, on eight numbers

raw_readings = [12, 15, 11, 14, 100, 102, 98, 101]     # imagine millions of these
summary = {
    "morning_avg": sum(raw_readings[:4]) / 4,
    "evening_avg": sum(raw_readings[4:]) / 4,
}
print(f"raw: {len(raw_readings)} numbers → summary: {len(summary)} numbers")
print(summary)

raw: 8 numbers → summary: 2 numbers
{'morning_avg': 13.0, 'evening_avg': 100.25}


Eight numbers became two, and the two are all a chart of “morning vs evening” would ever need. The next demo does the same reduction on 300,000 real rows.


30.2.2 Demo 14 — the size of what crosses the network

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

logs = pd.read_csv("datasets/request_logs.csv")

raw_mb = logs.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6
summary = logs.groupby(["hour", "status"]).agg(
    requests=("response_ms", "size"), avg_ms=("response_ms", "mean")).reset_index()
summary_kb = summary.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e3

print(f"raw data      : {len(logs):>10,} rows   {raw_mb:>8.1f} MB")
print(f"the summary   : {len(summary):>10,} rows   {summary_kb:>8.1f} KB")
print(f"reduction     : {raw_mb*1000/summary_kb:>10,.0f}× smaller\n")
print(summary.head(6).to_string(index=False))

30.3 10. Sampling honestly
A sampled chart is an estimate, and it must be labelled as one.

30.3.1 Demo 15 — a sample of four, from ten

import numpy as np

population = np.array([10, 12, 11, 50, 13, 9, 11, 48, 10, 12])
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
sample = rng.choice(population, 4, replace=False)

print(f"population mean : {population.mean():.1f}")
print(f"sample of 4     : {sample}, mean {sample.mean():.1f}")
print("\nA small sample can land on the outliers by chance and read high or low.")
print("The next demo shows how that risk shrinks as the sample grows.")

population mean : 18.6
sample of 4     : [11 13 12 50], mean 21.5

A small sample can land on the outliers by chance and read high or low.
The next demo shows how that risk shrinks as the sample grows.




30.3.2 Demo 16 — how wrong a sample can be, and how to say so

import numpy as np

population = pd.read_csv("datasets/sampling_population.csv")["value"].values
rng = np.random.default_rng(93)
truth = population.mean()

print(f"true mean over all {len(population):,} values: {truth:.3f}\n")
print(f"{'sample size':>12} {'estimate':>10} {'95% margin':>12} {'covers truth?':>15}")
print("-" * 54)
for size in [100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000]:
    s = rng.choice(population, size, replace=False)
    margin = 1.96 * s.std() / np.sqrt(size)
    covers = abs(s.mean() - truth) <= margin
    print(f"{size:>12,} {s.mean():>10.3f} {margin:>11.3f}  {'yes' if covers else 'no':>14}")

print("\nA sample of 10,000 estimates the mean of 300,000 to within a fraction of")
print("a percent. Sampling is not a compromise — it is usually the right answer.")

true mean over all 300,000 values: 79.925

 sample size   estimate   95% margin   covers truth?
------------------------------------------------------
         100     80.567      13.449             yes
       1,000     82.709       3.548             yes
      10,000     78.929       1.105             yes
     100,000     79.916       0.351             yes

A sample of 10,000 estimates the mean of 300,000 to within a fraction of
a percent. Sampling is not a compromise — it is usually the right answer.








Warning⚠️ Label every sampled chart



A chart built from a 1% sample looks exactly like one built from all the data. Put the sample size and the margin in the caption, or somebody will read a difference off it that is smaller than the sampling error.
And remember Session 2: a sample must be random. df.head(10000) is not a sample — it is whatever was written first, which is usually ordered by time or by ID.



import numpy as np, pandas as pd

# A real file, stored in signup order — and average spend has risen over time.
customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/customers_by_signup.csv")

print(f"true mean spend        : ₹{customers['spend'].mean():>7.0f}")
print(f"df.head(5000)          : ₹{customers['spend'].head(5000).mean():>7.0f}   ← earliest customers only")
print(f"df.sample(5000)        : ₹{customers['spend'].sample(5000, random_state=1).mean():>7.0f}   ← correct")

df.head(5000)          : ₹    209   ← earliest customers only

28.1 1. The project checklist
Before writing any code, answer four questions. A project that skips this stage usually produces a model nobody can use.








Question
A bad answer
A good answer




What decision changes?
“we want to understand customers”
“we decide who gets the retention offer”


What does success look like?
“high accuracy”
“catch 60% of churners while contacting under 20% of customers”


What data exists, and when?
“we have lots of data”
“12 months of transactions, available the day after”


What would make it useless?
—
“if it needs data we only have after the customer leaves”

28.2 2. Steps 1–3: clean, explore, prepare

28.2.1 Demo 3 — cleaning, with a report (Session 3)

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

def clean(df):
    report, d = {}, df.copy()
    report["rows_in"] = len(d)

    d = d.drop_duplicates()
    report["duplicates_removed"] = report["rows_in"] - len(d)

    bad = d["tenure_months"] < 0                       # impossible before missing
    report["impossible_values"] = int(bad.sum())
    d.loc[bad, "tenure_months"] = np.nan

    report["blanks_before"] = int(d[["monthly_spend", "tenure_months"]].isna().sum().sum())
    d["spend_was_missing"] = d["monthly_spend"].isna()
    d["monthly_spend"] = d["monthly_spend"].fillna(d["monthly_spend"].median())
    d["tenure_months"] = d["tenure_months"].fillna(d["tenure_months"].median())

    q1, q3 = d["monthly_spend"].quantile([.25, .75])
    report["outliers_flagged"] = int((d["monthly_spend"] > q3 + 1.5*(q3-q1)).sum())

    report["rows_out"] = len(d)
    report["blanks_after"] = int(d.isna().sum().sum())
    return d, report

clean_df, report = clean(customers)
print("CLEANING REPORT")
for k, v in report.items():
    print(f"  {k.replace('_',' '):<22} {v}")
print("\nOutliers were flagged, not removed — high spenders are real customers.")

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

28.3.1 Demo 6 — four models against a baseline (Sessions 9–11)

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score, roc_auc_score

cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
models = {
    "Baseline (majority)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Decision tree":       DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Random forest":       RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8,
                                                  random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Gradient boosting":   GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}

rows = []
for name, clf in models.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prepare), ("clf", clf)])
    cv_auc = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
    pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
    pred = pipe.predict(X_test)
    proba = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] if hasattr(clf, "predict_proba") else pred
    rows.append({
        "model": name,
        "cv_auc": f"{cv_auc.mean():.3f} ± {cv_auc.std():.3f}",
        "recall": round(recall_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), 3),
        "precision": round(precision_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), 3),
        "test_auc": round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3),
    })

print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Logistic regression 0.736 ± 0.053   0.685      0.180     0.742
      Decision tree 0.643 ± 0.031   0.575      0.209     0.671
      Random forest 0.683 ± 0.057   0.521      0.225     0.724

28.3.2 Demo 7 — the threshold is where the business requirement is met
Accuracy was never the goal. The goal was: catch 60% of churners while contacting under 30% of customers. That is a statement about the decision threshold, not the model.

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score

best = Pipeline([("prep", prepare),
                 ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8,
                                                random_state=0, class_weight="balanced"))])
best.fit(X_train, y_train)
proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

thresholds = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.025)
recalls  = [recall_score(y_test, proba >= t, zero_division=0) for t in thresholds]
contacts = [(proba >= t).mean() for t in thresholds]

plt.plot(thresholds, recalls, label="churners caught (recall)")
plt.plot(thresholds, contacts, label="customers contacted")
plt.axhline(0.60, color="green", ls="--", lw=1, label="required recall 0.60")
plt.axhline(0.30, color="red", ls="--", lw=1, label="contact budget 0.30")
plt.xlabel("decision threshold"); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

# Find every threshold that meets BOTH requirements at once.
met_requirement = []
for t, r, c in zip(thresholds, recalls, contacts):
    if r >= 0.60 and c <= 0.30:
        met_requirement.append((t, r, c))

if met_requirement:
    t, r, c = met_requirement[0]
    print(f"Requirement MET at threshold {t:.3f}: recall {r:.1%}, contacting {c:.1%}")
else:
    # No threshold meets both. Report the best recall among thresholds that
    # at least stay inside the 30% contact budget.
    best_recall_so_far = -1
    for t, r, c in zip(thresholds, recalls, contacts):
        if c <= 0.30 and r > best_recall_so_far:
            best_recall_so_far = r
            best_t, best_r, best_c = t, r, c
    print(f"Requirement NOT met by this model.")
    print(f"Within the 30% contact budget the best recall is "
          f"{best_r:.1%} at threshold {best_t:.3f}.")
    print("Report this honestly. Either the budget rises or the model improves.")







Figure 28.2: Recall and contact rate against the decision threshold. The shaded band is where both requirements hold.





Requirement NOT met by this model.
Within the 30% contact budget the best recall is 58.9% at threshold 0.450.
Report this honestly. Either the budget rises or the model improves.








Important🔓 Report against the requirement, not against 1.0



“AUC 0.78” is a number. “Catches 58.9% of churners within a 30% contact budget, against a target of 60%” is an answer. Only the second tells anyone whether to deploy.
Notice that this worked example does not meet its own target, and that this is left in rather than tidied away. That is the realistic outcome: a model with a respectable AUC can still fail the requirement the business actually set. The honest report says so and offers the two real options — raise the contact budget, or improve the model — instead of quietly switching to a metric that looks better.
A project that reports a missed target with the gap measured is worth more than one that reports a good-looking AUC against no target at all.

text:
29.1 4. Association rules
Association rule mining finds things that occur together. “People who buy bread and butter also buy jam.”
Written as a rule: {bread, butter} → {jam}. The left side is the antecedent, the right side the consequent.
Three numbers judge every rule. Compute them by hand once and they never confuse you again.








Measure
Question
Formula




Support
how often does this combination happen at all?
transactions with all items ÷ all transactions


Confidence
when the left side happens, how often does the right?
support(both) ÷ support(left)


Lift
is the right side more likely than usual when the left happens?
confidence ÷ support(right)



Lift is the one that matters:



Lift
Means




> 1
they go together more than chance — a real association


= 1
independent — the rule found nothing


< 1
they go together less than chance




29.1.1 Demo 8 — by hand, on ten baskets

# Ten baskets, one per line, from a real text file.
baskets = [set(line.split()) for line in
           open("datasets/baskets_small.txt").read().strip().split("\n")]
n = len(baskets)
for i, b in enumerate(baskets, 1):
    print(f"  basket {i:>2}: {sorted(b)}")
print()

def support(items):
    items = set(items)
    return sum(items <= b for b in baskets) / n

left, right = {"bread", "butter"}, {"jam"}

s_left  = support(left)
s_right = support(right)
s_both  = support(left | right)

confidence = s_both / s_left
lift       = confidence / s_right

print(f"Rule: {sorted(left)} → {sorted(right)}\n")
print(f"  support(bread & butter)       = {sum(left <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_left:.2f}")
print(f"  support(jam)                  = {sum(right <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_right:.2f}")
print(f"  support(all three together)   = {sum((left|right) <= b for b in baskets)}/{n} = {s_both:.2f}")
print(f"\n  confidence = {s_both:.2f} / {s_left:.2f} = {confidence:.2f}")
print(f"     → when someone buys bread and butter, {confidence:.0%} of the time they buy jam")
print(f"\n  lift = {confidence:.2f} / {s_right:.2f} = {lift:.2f}")
print(f"     → they are {lift:.2f}× more likely to buy jam than a random shopper")

  basket  1: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam']
  basket  2: ['bread', 'butter']
  basket  3: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam', 'milk']
  basket  4: ['eggs', 'milk']
  basket  5: ['bread', 'jam']
  basket  6: ['bread', 'butter', 'milk']
  basket  7: ['butter', 'jam']
  basket  8: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam']
  basket  9: ['bread', 'eggs', 'milk']
  basket 10: ['bread', 'butter', 'jam']

Rule: ['bread', 'butter'] → ['jam']

  support(bread & butter)       = 6/10 = 0.60
  support(jam)                  = 6/10 = 0.60
  support(all three together)   = 4/10 = 0.40

  confidence = 0.40 / 0.60 = 0.67
     → when someone buys bread and butter, 67% of the time they buy jam

  lift = 0.67 / 0.60 = 1.11
     → they are 1.11× more likely to buy jam than a random shopper




29.1.2 Demo 8 — the trap: high confidence, no information

# A rule about something almost everyone buys.
left2, right2 = {"milk"}, {"bread"}
c2 = support(left2 | right2) / support(left2)
l2 = c2 / support(right2)

print(f"Rule: milk → bread")
print(f"  confidence = {c2:.2f}   ← looks impressive")
print(f"  support(bread) = {support(right2):.2f}   ← but bread is in most baskets anyway")
print(f"  lift = {l2:.2f}")
print(f"\n  Lift near or below 1 means buying milk tells you NOTHING extra about bread.")
print(f"  A recommendation engine built on this rule would suggest bread to everybody.")

Rule: milk → bread
  confidence = 0.75   ← looks impressive
  support(bread) = 0.80   ← but bread is in most baskets anyway
  lift = 0.94

  Lift near or below 1 means buying milk tells you NOTHING extra about bread.
  A recommendation engine built on this rule would suggest bread to everybody.








Warning⚠️ Confidence alone will fool you



Any rule pointing at a very common item gets high confidence automatically. Always check lift, and be suspicious of any rule whose consequent is your best-selling product.

text:
29.2 5. Apriori on real-sized data
Checking every possible combination is impossible — 100 products give more than 10³⁰ possible itemsets. Apriori avoids that with one observation: if {bread, butter} is rare, then {bread, butter, jam} must be rarer still, so whole branches can be discarded without checking.

29.2.1 Demo 9 — mining rules with mlxtend

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules

# 4,000 real baskets. Three rules were planted when the file was generated,
# so we can check the algorithm against a truth we know — see
# datasets/make_session_16.py.
raw = pd.read_csv("datasets/grocery_baskets.csv")
transactions = [set(items.split(",")) for items in raw["items"]]
products = sorted({p for t in transactions for p in t})
print(f"{len(transactions):,} baskets, {len(products)} distinct products\n")

onehot = pd.DataFrame([{p: (p in t) for p in products} for t in transactions])

frequent = apriori(onehot, min_support=0.05, use_colnames=True)
# Deliberately NO lift floor here, so we can see how many worthless rules
# a permissive search produces.
rules = association_rules(frequent, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.10)
rules = rules.sort_values("lift", ascending=False)

print(f"{len(transactions):,} baskets → {len(frequent)} frequent itemsets → {len(rules)} rules\n")
out = rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift"]].head(8).copy()
out["antecedents"] = out["antecedents"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(s)))
out["consequents"] = out["consequents"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(sorted(s)))
print(out.round(3).to_string(index=False))

4,000 baskets, 10 distinct products

4,000 baskets → 34 frequent itemsets → 56 rules

      bread      butter    0.171       0.832 2.483
     butter       bread    0.171       0.510 2.483
butter, jam       bread    0.116       0.487 2.375
      bread butter, jam    0.116       0.564 2.375

29.2.2 Demo 10 — did it find the rules we planted?

planted = [({"bread"}, {"butter"}), ({"butter"}, {"jam"}), ({"coffee"}, {"sugar"})]

print("Checking the algorithm against the truth we built in:\n")
for ante, cons in planted:
    hit = rules[(rules["antecedents"] == frozenset(ante)) &
                (rules["consequents"] == frozenset(cons))]
    if len(hit):
        r = hit.iloc[0]
        print(f"  FOUND   {sorted(ante)} → {sorted(cons)}   "
              f"confidence {r['confidence']:.2f}  lift {r['lift']:.2f}")
    else:
        print(f"  MISSED  {sorted(ante)} → {sorted(cons)}")

useless = rules[rules["lift"] < 1.1]
print(f"\n{len(useless)} of {len(rules)} rules have lift below 1.1 — they tell you")
print("nothing, however good their confidence looks.")
if len(useless):
    worst = useless.sort_values("confidence", ascending=False).iloc[0]
    print(f"  worst offender: {sorted(worst['antecedents'])} → {sorted(worst['consequents'])}")
    print(f"  confidence {worst['confidence']:.2f}, but lift {worst['lift']:.2f} — below 1, so buying")
    print(f"  the antecedent makes the consequent LESS likely than for a random shopper")
print("\nFilter on lift FIRST, then read the survivors.")

section: 30.1 6. Test the claim, do not just draw it
text:
30.1 6. Test the claim, do not just draw it
A box plot showing two groups apart is a hypothesis, not a finding. The gap might be sampling noise. A statistical test puts a number on how likely that is.



Question
Test




Do two groups differ in a number?
t-test


Are two categories related?
chi-square


Do three or more groups differ?
ANOVA



The p-value is the probability of seeing a gap this large if there were genuinely no difference. Small p-value → the gap is unlikely to be chance.






Warning⚠️ What a p-value does not mean



It is not the probability that your hypothesis is true. It is not a measure of how big or important the effect is — with 100,000 rows, a trivial difference produces a tiny p-value.
Always report the effect size next to the p-value. “Churners make 1.4 more support calls on average (p < 0.001)” is a finding. “p < 0.001” alone is not.



30.1.1 Demo 11 — testing the three hypotheses from Demo 3

from scipy import stats
import pandas as pd

churned  = clean_df[clean_df["churned"] == 1]
retained = clean_df[clean_df["churned"] == 0]

print("t-tests: do churners and retained customers differ?\n")
for col in ["support_calls", "tenure_months", "monthly_spend"]:
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(churned[col], retained[col], equal_var=False)
    diff = churned[col].mean() - retained[col].mean()
    # Cohen's d — how big the difference is, in standard deviations
    pooled = ((churned[col].std()**2 + retained[col].std()**2) / 2) ** 0.5
    d = diff / pooled
    verdict = "REAL" if p < 0.05 else "not significant"
    size = "large" if abs(d) > .8 else "medium" if abs(d) > .5 else "small" if abs(d) > .2 else "negligible"
    print(f"  {col:<16} difference {diff:>+8.2f}   p = {p:<10.2e} {verdict:<16} effect: {size} (d={d:+.2f})")

# chi-square: is churn related to the plan a customer is on?
table = pd.crosstab(clean_df["plan"], clean_df["churned"])
chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(f"\nchi-square, plan vs churn: χ² = {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.2e}")
print(f"  → plan and churn are {'related' if p < 0.05 else 'independent'}")
print(table.to_string())

t-tests: do churners and retained customers differ?

  tenure_months    difference   -11.54   p = 4.02e-20   REAL             effect: medium (d=-0.59)
  monthly_spend    difference   -35.60   p = 2.85e-01   not significant  effect: negligible (d=-0.06)

chi-square, plan vs churn: χ² = 38.0, p = 5.72e-09

plan

31.1 7. What you hand over







Deliverable
Must contain




Repository
code that runs from a clean clone, requirements.txt with versions pinned, a seed everywhere

the question, what you did, what you found, and what you could not conclude


Model bundle
the full pipeline plus its metadata (Session 12)

Presentation
eight minutes: problem, approach, result, limitations




31.1.1 Demo 13 — packaging the result (Session 12)

import joblib, sklearn, tempfile, os, json
import numpy as np
from datetime import date
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score, roc_auc_score

folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path = os.path.join(folder, "churn_model.joblib")

proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
thresholds = np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.025)
viable = [(t, recall_score(y_test, proba >= t), (proba >= t).mean())
          for t in thresholds if (proba >= t).mean() <= 0.30]
chosen_t, chosen_recall, chosen_contact = max(viable, key=lambda z: z[1])

bundle = {
    "pipeline": best,
    "features": features,
    "decision_threshold": round(float(chosen_t), 3),
    "trained_on": str(date.today()),
    "n_training_rows": int(len(X_train)),
    "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__,
    "test_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)), 3),
    "recall_at_threshold": round(float(chosen_recall), 3),
    "contact_rate_at_threshold": round(float(chosen_contact), 3),
    "target_recall": 0.60,
    "contact_budget": 0.30,
    "known_limitations": [
        "trained on 12 months only; no seasonal effects captured",
        "support_calls is recorded after a complaint, so very recent calls may be missing",
        "no data on competitor pricing, which is likely a real driver",
    ],
}
joblib.dump(bundle, path)

loaded = joblib.load(path)
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in loaded.items() if k != "pipeline"}, indent=2))

text:
31.2 8. Responsible delivery
Before a model touches a real person, answer three questions in writing.







Question
For this project




Who could be harmed by a wrong prediction?
a loyal customer wrongly flagged gets an unnecessary discount — cheap. A churner missed is a lost customer — the expensive error, which is why recall was the target.


Does it treat groups differently?
check the error rate per city and per plan, not just overall


Would you be comfortable explaining a decision to the person it affected?
if the answer needs “component 1 was low”, reconsider (Session 6)




31.2.1 Demo 14 — a fairness check

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score

check = X_test.copy()
check["actual"] = y_test.values
check["predicted"] = (best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] >= chosen_t).astype(int)

print("Does the model perform equally across groups?\n")
for group in ["city", "plan"]:
    print(f"By {group}:")
    for value, sub in check.groupby(group):
        if sub["actual"].sum() == 0:
            continue
        print(f"  {value:<10} n={len(sub):>4}  "
              f"recall {recall_score(sub['actual'], sub['predicted'], zero_division=0):.2f}  "
              f"contacted {sub['predicted'].mean():.1%}")
    print()

recalls = [recall_score(s["actual"], s["predicted"], zero_division=0)
           for _, s in check.groupby("city") if s["actual"].sum() > 0]
print(f"Recall ranges from {min(recalls):.2f} to {max(recalls):.2f} across cities.")
print("A large gap means the model serves some groups better than others —")
print("worth investigating before anyone acts on it.")

Does the model perform equally across groups?

By city:
